                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "The problem isn't access to `repos.Instance` — that part is fine. `Instance` is exported (capital `I`) and the import path is correct. The actual issue is a **syntax error** in how you're using it inside the struct literal.\n\nLook at `initialModel()`:\n\n```go\nfunc initialModel() model {\n\treturn model{\n\t\t// Our to-do list is a grocery list\n\t\trepos.Instance.Get()          // ← this is invalid here\n\t\tchoices: []string{\"Buy carrots\", \"Buy celery\", \"Buy kohlrabi\"},\n\t\tselected: make(map[int]struct{}),\n\t}\n}\n```\n\nYou've dropped a bare statement (`repos.Instance.Get()`) inside a composite literal. Inside `model{ ... }` Go only accepts `field: value` elements separated by commas — you can't put an arbitrary function call there. That's what makes the compiler choke, and it can look like `repos.Instance` \"can't be accessed.\"\n\nThere are two things to sort out:\n\n1. `repos.Instance.Get()` returns a `map[string]string`, but your `model.choices` field is `[]string`. So you need to decide what you actually want from it — presumably the repo keys as the list of choices.\n2. `Instance` is only non-nil after `repos.Init()` has been called. Make sure `Init()` runs (in `main.go`) before the UI program starts, otherwise `repos.Instance` will be `nil` and you'll get a nil-pointer panic at runtime.\n\nHere's a corrected `initialModel()` that turns the repo map keys into the choices:\n\n```go\nfunc initialModel() model {\n\trepoMap := repos.Instance.Get()\n\n\tchoices := make([]string, 0, len(repoMap))\n\tfor key := range repoMap {\n\t\tchoices = append(choices, key)\n\t}\n\n\treturn model{\n\t\tchoices:  choices,\n\t\tselected: make(map[int]struct{}),\n\t}\n}\n```\n\nWant me to apply this change to `ui/ui.go`? If so, I'd also like to check `main.go` to confirm `repos.Init()` is called before `ui.CreateProgram()`."

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Let me look at how the map is currently populated and used to answer this properly.\n\nLooking at the current `loadRepos()` parsing:\n\n```go\nkey, value, found := strings.Cut(line, \"#\")\nif !found {\n    value = key\n}\nr.repoMap[key] = value\n```\n\nAnd the file format from `sync()`:\n```go\nif value == key {\n    fmt.Fprintf(&builder, \"%s\\n\", key)      // no '#' when value == key\n} else {\n    fmt.Fprintf(&builder, \"%s#%s\\n\", key, value)\n}\n```\n\nSo the current line format is `key#value`. The question is really about what semantics you want each column to have.\n\nHere's the thing: your map is **already** effectively `key → value`. The question of \"which is the alias and which is the path\" is about what you *store* in each, not about restructuring the map itself. So the real question is which direction gives you the lookups you need.\n\nConsider how you'll actually use it:\n\n- **alias → path** (key = alias, value = path): natural for a `taco` CLI. The user types an alias like `taco myproject` and you look up the path. Map lookup by key is O(1), which is exactly the hot path. `GetValue(alias)` returns the path directly. This is almost certainly what you want.\n\n- **path → alias** (key = path, value = alias): you'd only want this if your primary lookup is \"given a path, what's its alias?\" — much rarer for a navigation tool.\n\nSo yes — **key = alias, value = path** is the better design for a repo-jumping CLI. And it fits your other question: `Get()` returning the values then gives you the list of paths, while the keys give you the human-friendly aliases to display.\n\nOne consequence worth noting: the current `value == key` shorthand (writing just `alias` with no `#` when they're equal) still works fine — it'd mean \"alias equals path,\" which is a slightly odd case but harmless.\n\nDo you want me to:\n1. Just proceed with the `initialModel()` fix (collecting values = paths), keeping the current `alias#path` format, or\n2. Also add a helper or adjust anything in `repos.go` to make the alias/path intent explicit (e.g. renaming for clarity, or displaying `alias` in the UI but selecting the `path`)?\n\nMy recommendation is option 2's display idea for the UI: show the alias in the list but keep the path associated, so selecting an item can navigate.                   {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "It's a reasonable direction, and the instinct to model a repo as its own struct is good. But there are two Go-specific issues with `map[Repo]Session` as described, plus a design question worth settling before you build it.\n\n**1. Using a struct as a map key**\n\n`map[Repo]Session` is legal *only* if `Repo` is comparable (no slices/maps/funcs inside). It'd work if `Repo` is just `{ Alias, Path string }`. But keying by the struct value is fragile: if any repo field changes, the key changes, and you lose the entry. Aliases are your natural unique identifier, so keying by `string` (alias) is simpler and more robust. Most Go code keys by an ID field rather than the whole struct.\n\n**2. \"values will be null until we create sessions\"**\n\nGo has no null for a struct value type. A `map[...]Session` always holds a fully-zeroed `Session` for every key — you can't distinguish \"no session yet\" from \"a zero session.\" The idiomatic fix is a **pointer**: `*Session`, where `nil` genuinely means \"no session yet.\" That gives you exactly the \"loaded key, empty value\" semantics you want.\n\n**3. The design question: is a repo→session a map at all?**\n\nYou said keys load at startup and values fill in later. That's not really a lookup table — it's a fixed set of repos, each of which *has an optional session*. That's more naturally modeled as the session living *inside* the repo:\n\n```go\ntype Session struct {\n    Name string\n    // tmux session details...\n}\n\ntype Repo struct {\n    Alias   string\n    Path    string\n    Session *Session // nil until a session is started\n}\n```\n\nThen your global becomes `map[string]*Repo` (keyed by alias), or even just `[]*Repo` since you display them as a list anyway. At startup you load repos with `Session: nil`; when the user starts one, you set `repo.Session = &Session{...}`.\n\n**Why I'd prefer this over `map[Repo]Session`:**\n- Each repo carries its own session state — no parallel map to keep in sync.\n- `nil` cleanly means \"no session,\" which is exactly your requirement.\n- Keying by alias (or a slice) avoids the fragile-struct-key problem.\n- Your TUI already lists aliases; iterating `[]*Repo` to render alias + \"running?\" indicator is trivial.\n\n**How it maps onto what's there now:** your current `repoMap map[string]string` (alias → path) becomes `map[string]*Repo` (alias → repo), and the path moves inside `Repo`. `Keys()` still returns aliases for the list. `loadRepos()` builds `*Repo` values with `Session: nil`.\n\nOne thing to decide: do you need lookup-by-alias frequently (e.g. \"user selected alias X, attach its session\")? If yes, keep the `map[string]*Repo`. If you only ever iterate for display and selection-by-index, a `[]*Repo` is even simpler.\n\nWant me to sketch the refactor of `repos.go` to this shape (a `Repo` struct with an optional `*Session`, map keyed by alias)? I'd keep `Get`/`Keys`/`GetValue` working so `ui.go` and `main.go` don't break, then we can wire sessions in incrementally."
                  }

                    "data": "Builds and vets cleanly. Here's the new shape:\n\n**`session/session.go`** — a `Session` struct (currently just `Name`; expand with tmux details as you wire it up).\n\n**`repos/repos.go`** — the core change:\n```go\ntype Repo struct {\n\tAlias   string\n\tPath    string\n\tSession *session.Session // nil until a session is started\n}\n```\nThe global is now a `[]*Repo` list (`Repos.list`), loaded at startup with `Session: nil`.                     "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Good catch — you're right that `path` and `alias` now live on each `Repo`, so `Repos` no longer holds anything repo-shaped. But it's not empty: it still carries the persistence `path` (where `~/.taco/repositories` lives) plus the `list` itself. The real question is whether that wrapper earns its keep.\n\nTwo viable shapes:\n\n**Option A — drop the `Repos` struct, use a package-level slice.**\n```go\nvar Instance []*Repo\nvar reposFilePath string // where the list persists\n```\nFunctions become package-level: `repos.Aliases()`, `repos.Find(alias)`, `repos.Add(...)`. Callers get `repos.Instance` as the raw `[]*Repo`. Simpler, less ceremony — fits a singleton that there's only ever one of.\n\n**Option B — keep the `Repos` struct (current).**\nIt groups the slice with its file path and hangs the methods off a receiver. The value is mostly cohesion: the persistence detail (`path`) stays bundled with the data it persists, rather than floating as a package-level var.\n\nThe distinction that matters: `Repos` isn't standing in for a repo — it's the *collection + its storage location*. So it's not redundant with `Repo`. Whether it's worth a struct comes down to taste and whether you'll ever want more than one collection.\n\nMy honest read for this project: it's a global singleton, there's exactly one repo list, and the only extra state is the file path. That's a textbook case where a struct adds ceremony without payoff — **Option A is the cleaner fit**. You keep `Repo` as the real struct, and the collection is just `[]*Repo` with a couple of package functions.\n\nThe one thing you'd lose is method syntax (`repos.Instance.Find(x)` becomes `repos.Find(x)`), which is arguably nicer anyway.\n\nWant me to flatten it to Option A — package-level `Instance []*Repo` plus `Aliases`/`Find`/`Add`/`Delete` as package functions, and update `ui.go`/`main.go` to match?"
                  }

                    "data": "Builds and vets cleanly. `Session` now has a unique `ID` instead of a name:\n\n```go\ntype Session struct {\n\tID string // unique, tmux-safe identifier\n}\n\nfunc New() *Session // generates a fresh ID\n```\n\nThe ID is a 16-char hex string from `crypto/rand` — no new dependencies, and it's safe to use directly as a tmux session target in your `commands.go` templates (no `.` or `:` characters).\n\nStarting a session for a repo becomes:\n\n```go\nrepo := repos.Find(alias)\nrepo.Session = session.New()\n// then: commands.CreateSession(repo.Session.ID, repo.Path)\n```\n\nTwo things you may want to decide later:\n- If you need sessions to **survive a restart** (reattach to tmux sessions that are still alive), the ID has to be persisted alongside the repo — right now `Session` is in-memory only and the repositories file doesn't store it.\n- If you also want a human-readable label separate from the ID, add a `Name` field back.                   {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Short answer: no — Lip Gloss doesn't have a global \"theme\" or an ambient stylesheet that automatically applies to everything. It's not like CSS with cascading rules that hit every element. In Lip Gloss you create explicit `Style` values and you have to actually call `.Render(...)` on each string you want styled. If a piece of text never passes through a style, it stays plain. There's no auto-application.\n\nSo there's no switch that says \"style all components.\" What people *do* to get that effect is a deliberate pattern:\n\n1. **Define a theme in one place** — a struct or set of package-level `Style` variables (colors, borders, active/inactive, help text, etc.). One source of truth.\n2. **Route all rendering through it** — every render function pulls from that theme rather than styling ad hoc. Change the theme once, and everything that uses it updates.\n\nThat gets you the *practical* outcome you're describing — consistent styling everywhere, tweakable from one spot — but it's convention, not automatic. Each render site still has to opt in by using the shared styles.\n\nThere is one thing that *is* global-ish: Lip Gloss can detect the terminal's color profile and light/dark background and adapt colors automatically (`AdaptiveColor` and background detection). But that adapts *which* colors resolve to — it still only affects text you've explicitly styled.\n\nGiven your code, the clean way to do this is:\n\n- A `theme.go` (or a `styles` struct) holding all the `lipgloss.Style` definitions.\n- `renderTabBar`, `renderReposTab`, `renderPlaceholder`, and the outer panel in `View()` all draw from it.\n\nSince your whole UI already funnels through a handful of `render*` helpers in one file, wiring them all to a shared theme is small and gives you effectively \"one place controls the look of everything.\"\n\nWant me to set it up that way — add Lip Gloss v2, create a single shared theme, and route all the existing render functions through it? That's the closest you get to \"applied automatically everywhere.\""
                  }
                ],

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Not quite — that's an important distinction, and it depends on what you mean by \"styled components.\"\n\nLip Gloss doesn't have \"components.\" A `lipgloss.Style` is a **reusable style definition**, not a finished piece of UI. It's a recipe (border + color + padding), and you apply it to text at render time with `.Render(\"some text\")`. The actual content is still supplied by the caller each frame, because your content changes every frame (cursor moves, active tab changes, repo list, etc.).\n\nSo there are really two things `theme.go` could export, and they serve different purposes:\n\n**1. Styles (the recipe) — this is the normal, recommended approach.**\n```go\n// theme.go\nvar (\n    ActiveTab   = lipgloss.NewStyle().Border(...).Foreground(...)\n    InactiveTab = lipgloss.NewStyle().Faint(true)\n    Panel       = lipgloss.NewStyle().Border(lipgloss.RoundedBorder())\n    SelectedRow = lipgloss.NewStyle().Reverse(true)\n    Help        = lipgloss.NewStyle().Faint(true)\n)\n```\nThen render sites feed content in:\n```go\nActiveTab.Render(\"Repos\")\nSelectedRow.Render(alias)\n```\nThe style is fixed and shared; the text is dynamic. This is exactly the \"one place controls the look\" pattern.\n\n**2. Helper functions (styled renderers) — optional convenience on top.**\nIf you'd rather callers not call `.Render` themselves, `theme.go` can wrap styles in functions:\n```go\nfunc Tab(label string, active bool) string {\n    if active {\n        return ActiveTab.Render(label)\n    }\n    return InactiveTab.Render(label)\n}\nfunc Panel(content string) string { ... }\n```\nNow the rest of the app calls `theme.Tab(\"Repos\", true)` and never touches Lip Gloss directly. These *feel* like \"styled components ready to use,\" but under the hood they're just functions that take content and return a styled string.\n\nWhat you **can't** export is a fully self-contained widget that knows its own content and re-renders itself — that's the job of the Bubbles library (the `list`, `table`, etc. components), which is a separate thing from styling.\n\nMy recommendation for your codebase: export **styles** (option 1) plus a few small **helper functions** (option 2) for the repeated pieces (tab, panel, selected row). That gives you clean call sites like `theme.Tab(...)` and `theme.Panel(...)` while keeping a single source of truth.                   {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Good question, and the answer differs depending on whether the \"fancy\" component is something you write or something from the Bubbles library — because those two get themed in different ways.\n\n**Case 1: a component you write yourself (like your repos menu).**\nSame pattern you already have. The component's render function takes content and calls the shared theme helpers/styles from `theme.go`. Nothing new — you just make sure the new render code pulls from `theme.go` instead of defining its own `lipgloss.NewStyle()` inline. That's the discipline that keeps \"one place controls the look.\"\n\n**Case 2: a Bubbles component (e.g. the `list` bubble — the actual \"list-fancy\" example).**\nThis is the important distinction: Bubbles components own their own styling internally. You don't render them by passing text through your `Row(...)` helper — instead each Bubble exposes a **`Styles` struct** (and often a `Delegate` for lists) that you populate with `lipgloss.Style` values. So \"make it use the theme\" means: build that component's `Styles` struct **from your theme's palette/styles**, rather than letting it use its defaults.\n\nConcretely, the flow for the Bubbles `list`:\n\n```go\nimport \"github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles/list\"  // note: separate lib\n\n// In theme.go — derive the list's styles from your palette:\nfunc ListStyles() list.Styles {\n    s := list.DefaultStyles()\n    s.Title = s.Title.Background(colorAccent)      // reuse your palette\n    s.PaginationStyle = s.PaginationStyle.Foreground(colorMuted)\n    // ...override the bits you care about\n    return s\n}\n\n// And the item delegate controls how each row looks:\nfunc ListDelegate() list.DefaultDelegate {\n    d := list.NewDefaultDelegate()\n    d.Styles.SelectedTitle = d.Styles.SelectedTitle.Foreground(colorAccent)\n    d.Styles.NormalTitle = d.Styles.NormalTitle // etc.\n    return d\n}\n```\n\nThen in the model you construct the list once and inject those:\n```go\nl := list.New(items, ListDelegate(), width, height)\nl.Styles = ListStyles()\n```\n\nSo the theming boundary is: **your theme exports the palette + a few `*Styles()` constructor functions; the Bubble consumes them.** The palette (`colorAccent`, `colorMuted`, `colorBorder`) stays the single source of truth — both your hand-rolled `Row(...)` and the Bubbles list's styles read from it, so they stay visually consistent.\n\nTwo practical caveats before you add it:\n\n1. **Version namespace.** Your project uses the `charm.land/*` **v2** generation. The Bubbles `list` most commonly documented is `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles` (v1), which pairs with the old `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea` v1 — mixing generations won't compile. I'd need to check whether there's a `charm.land/bubbles` (v2) that matches your `charm.land/bubbletea/v2` before adding it. Let me verify that when you're ready.\n\n2. **It replaces, not layers.** The Bubbles `list` is a full component with its own `Update`/`View` — you'd delegate key events to it (`list.Update(msg)`) and render `list.View()` inside your panel, rather than your current manual cursor + `Row(...)` loop.\n\nRecommended path: keep the palette in `theme.go` as the source of truth, and for each Bubbles component add a `XxxStyles()` constructor in `theme.go` that builds its style struct from the palette. That mirrors your current setup and keeps everything consistent.\n\nWant me to check whether a v2-compatible Bubbles `list` exists in your module cache, and if so, wire it into the Repos tab with a `theme.go` styles constructor?"

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Yes — that's exactly the \"fullscreen\" mechanism bubbletea provides. In your `View()`:\n\n```go\nv := tea.NewView(content)\nv.AltScreen = true   // ← this is bubbletea's fullscreen\nreturn v\n```\n\n`AltScreen` switches the terminal into its **alternate screen buffer** — the same thing `vim`, `less`, and `htop` use. That's what \"fullscreen\" means in bubbletea: the program takes over the entire terminal window and, on quit, restores your previous shell contents. So we are using bubbletea's built-in fullscreen, not faking it.\n\nOne clarification worth making, because \"fullscreen\" can mean two separate things and they're easy to conflate:\n\n1. **Taking over the window (alt screen)** — handled entirely by `v.AltScreen = true`. Bubbletea does this for you.\n\n2. **Filling that window with content** — bubbletea does *not* do this. It just prints whatever string your `View()` returns. If your content is shorter than the screen, the rest is blank. That's why we capture `tea.WindowSizeMsg` (`m.width`/`m.height`) and size the panel with `Panel(body, m.width, panelHeight)` so the bordered box actually spans the window.\n\nSo the division is: bubbletea gives you the fullscreen *canvas* (alt screen), and your `View()` + Lip Gloss sizing is what *fills* that canvas. Both pieces are in place right now.\n\nFor contrast: in bubbletea **v1** you'd request fullscreen with a program option (`tea.NewProgram(m, tea.WithAltScreen())`). In your **v2** version that option was removed — it's now the `AltScreen` field on the `View`, which is what we're using. So we're doing it the idiomatic v2 way."
                  }

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "`tea.ExecProcess` is exactly the tool — it pauses bubbletea, hands the terminal to the child (tmux), and resumes when tmux exits. The doc even cites spawning interactive shells as the use case. This is the correct, idiomatic path.\n\nNow the plan:\n\n**Flow on Enter:** get the selected repo → build a tmux command that creates the session if it doesn't exist and attaches to it → run it via `tea.ExecProcess` → when tmux exits (user detaches), bubbletea resumes.\n\nI'll use `tmux new-session -A -s <id> -c <path>` — the `-A` flag means \"attach if the session exists, otherwise create it,\" which collapses create+attach into one atomic, interactive command. That's cleaner than create-then-attach as two steps and avoids race/ordering bugs. I'll keep your fancy escape-binding script but run the whole thing through `sh -c`.\n\nLet me fix `commands.go` first:"
                  },
                  {
                    "kind": "toolUse",
                    "data": {
                      "toolUseId": "toolu_bdrk_01Vr2x1QtwTdViLfxLs7Gn2b",
                      "name": "write",

                        "__tool_use_purpose": "Fix exec usage (run via shell) and add a create-or-attach command.",
                        "command": "create",
                        "content": "package commands\n\nimport (\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"os/exec\"\n)\n\n// createOrAttachTemplate creates the tmux session if it does not exist and\n// attaches to it (the -A flag). The inner bindings configure escape/detach\n// behaviour and mouse support. %s placeholders are session id and directory.\nconst createOrAttachTemplate = `tmux new-session -A -s %s -c %s \\\n   \"tmux bind-key -n Escape run 'if \\\n   [ #{pane_current_command} != vi ] && \\\n   [ #{pane_current_command} != vim ] && \\\n   [ #{pane_current_command} != nvim ] && \\\n   [ #{pane_current_command} != k9s ] && \\\n   [ #{pane_current_command} != git ]; \\\n   then tmux detach; \\\n   else tmux send-keys Escape; fi'; \\\n   tmux set-option -g escape-time 0; \\\n   tmux set -g mouse on; \\\n   zsh\"`\n\nconst attachTemplate = `tmux attach -t %s`\nconst terminateTemplate = `tmux kill-session -t %s`\n\n// CreateOrAttachSession returns a command that creates the tmux session named\n// sessionID (rooted at directory) if needed and attaches to it. It is an\n// interactive command intended to be run via tea.ExecProcess, which hands the\n// terminal to tmux while the bubbletea program is suspended.\nfunc CreateOrAttachSession(sessionID string, directory string) *exec.Cmd {\n\tscript := fmt.Sprintf(createOrAttachTemplate, sessionID, directory)\n\treturn exec.Command(\"sh\", \"-c\", script)\n}\n\n// AttachToSession attaches to an existing tmux session. Interactive; run via\n// tea.ExecProcess.\nfunc AttachToSession(sessionID string) *exec.Cmd {\n\tscript := fmt.Sprintf(attachTemplate, sessionID)\n\treturn exec.Command(\"sh\", \"-c\", script)\n}\n\n// TerminateSession kills a tmux session. Non-interactive; can run directly.\nfunc TerminateSession(sessionID string) *exec.Cmd {\n\tscript := fmt.Sprintf(terminateTemplate, sessionID)\n\treturn exec.Command(\"sh\", \"-c\", script)\n}\n",

                    "data": "Builds and vets cleanly. Here's what pressing Enter now does:\n\n1. Finds the repo under the cursor via `repos.Find(alias)`.\n2. If the repo has no session yet (`repo.Session == nil`), it creates one (`session.New()`, generating a unique ID) and runs your original `CREATE_SESSION_COMMAND` (which creates *and* attaches). If a session already exists, it runs `ATTACH_SESSION_COMMAND` instead.\n3. Runs that command through **`tea.ExecProcess`**, which suspends the bubbletea UI, hands the full terminal over to tmux (so all your escape/mouse bindings and `zsh` work normally), and resumes the UI when you detach.\n4.                   {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Builds and vets cleanly. The cleanup covers three exit paths:\n\n1. **Normal quit / Ctrl+C** — bubbletea catches SIGINT itself and returns from `program.Run()`, so `defer terminateAllSessions()` handles both. This is the common case.\n2. **SIGTERM (and SIGINT outside the UI loop)** — a `signal.Notify` goroutine runs cleanup and exits, as a backstop for signals bubbletea doesn't consume.\n3. **Run error** — cleanup runs explicitly before exiting.\n\nA `sync.Once` guards `terminateAllSessions` so it runs at most once even if two paths fire (e.g. signal handler + defer). It iterates `repos.WithSessions()` (the new accessor returning repos with `Session != nil`) and runs your `TERMINATE_SESSION_COMMAND` for each.\n\nTwo honest caveats:\n\n- **I can't run this** — it needs a real TTY and tmux, which I don't have here. Please test: launch a session with Enter, detach, then quit taco (both `q` and Ctrl+C), and verify with `tmux ls` that the session is gone.\n- **One race worth knowing:** the signal goroutine calls `os.Exit(1)` immediately after cleanup. If a signal arrives *while you're attached inside tmux*, bubbletea is suspended (via `ExecProcess`) and the signal behavior gets murkier — the signal may go to tmux/the foreground process group rather than taco. In practice Ctrl+C while inside tmux goes to whatever's running in the tmux pane, not taco, so this mainly matters for an external `kill`. That's an edge case; the primary quit-from-UI path is solid.\n\nThere's also a limitation inherent to the approach: `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`) and power loss can never be trapped, so a session could survive those. If you want taco to clean up *orphaned* sessions from a previous run, that needs the persisted-session-ID approach I mentioned earlier (check `tmux has-session` at startup and reap stragglers). Want me to add that, or is trapping the normal exit paths enough for now?"
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Builds and vets cleanly. The indicator now sits on the right: each alias is padded out to a column at `longest_alias_length + 5`, and the `●` (or a blank for inactive) is drawn there. Because the column is computed from the longest alias across all rows, every indicator lines up in the same vertical column.\n\nSo a list like:\n\n```\n  api            ●\n  web-dashboard  ●\n  tools\n```\n\nwith the dots aligned 5 spaces past the longest alias (`web-dashboard`).\n\nTwo caveats worth noting:\n- The alignment uses `len(alias)`, which counts bytes, not display width. For plain ASCII aliases that's identical to visible width. If you ever use non-ASCII/multi-byte aliases, the column could drift — Lip Gloss has a width function that measures display cells if you need it later.\n- Verify visually with `go run .` since I can't render it here.\n\nWant the indicator to only reserve/show the column when at least one session is active, or is the always-aligned column fine?"

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Builds and vets cleanly. The list (and the placeholder text on the other tabs) is now centered both horizontally and vertically inside the panel via `PanelCentered`, which uses `lipgloss.Place` within the panel's inner area.\n\nI also fixed a latent sizing bug while I was in there: the old `Panel` subtracted only `2` from the width but the box actually costs border(2) + padding(4) horizontally, so it was rendering wider than intended (likely overflowing on narrower terminals). `Panel` now computes the true inner content area, and `panelInner` centralizes that math so `PanelCentered` places content into the exact available space.\n\nOne thing worth deciding: the whole list block is centered as a unit, so the list stays left-aligned *within itself* (rows share a left edge) but the block sits in the middle of the box. That's usually what \"list in the middle\" means and keeps the indicator column alignment intact. If instead you wanted each row individually centered, that would break the indicator column — so I went with block-centering. \n\nVerify with `go run .` since I can't render it. Want the tab body vertically centered only (list kept at the left margin horizontally), or is fully-centered as-is what you're after?"
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Short answer: no — a terminal program can't change font size. Text size is controlled entirely by the user's terminal emulator (iTerm2, Alacritty, etc.) and their font settings, not by anything the program can emit. There's no escape sequence or Lip Gloss option for \"bigger text\" the way there is for color or bold. So bubbletea/Lip Gloss fundamentally can't do it.\n\nWhat you *can* do to make things read as bigger or bolder within those constraints:\n\n1. **Bold** — you're already using it on active tabs and selected rows. It's the closest thing to \"heavier\" text.\n\n2. **FIGlet-style ASCII banners** — render text as large multi-line glyphs built out of regular characters. This is how CLI tools show big titles. Charm has a library for exactly this that pairs with your v2 stack. It only makes sense for short strings (a title, a logo, maybe a single selected item), not a whole scrollable list — a repo list rendered in giant letters would overflow instantly.\n\n3. **A minor terminal trick:** some terminals support a \"double-height line\" DEC escape (`ESC # 3` / `ESC # 4`), but support is spotty (works in xterm, not in many modern emulators) and Lip Gloss doesn't manage it, so it's fragile. I wouldn't rely on it.\n\nLet me check whether the big-text library is available in your module cache so option 2 is actually on the table:"
                  },
                  {
                    "kind": "toolUse",
                    "data": {
                      "toolUseId": "toolu_bdrk_01JCmTwagtyG9knKZijgDnkH",
                      "name": "shell",
                      "input": {
                        "__tool_use_purpose": "Check for a figlet/big-text library compatible with the charm.land v2 stack.",
                        "command": "ls $(go env GOMODCACHE)/charm.land 2>/dev/null; echo \"=== x ===\"; ls $(go env GOMODCACHE)/charm.land/x 2>/dev/null; echo \"=== figlet-ish ===\"; ls $(go env GOMODCACHE)/github.com/charmbracelet 2>/dev/null; find $(go env GOMODCACHE) -maxdepth 3 -iname \"*figlet*\" 2>/dev/null | head",
                        "working_dir": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco"
                      }
                    }
                  }

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Search is wired in. Summary of the new behavior:\n\n**Keys (letters freed for search):**\n- `↑`/`↓` — navigate the filtered list\n- `←`/`→` (or `Tab`/`Shift+Tab`) — switch tabs\n- Any printable character — appended to the search query\n- `Backspace` — delete last char; `Esc` — clear query\n- `Enter` — launch selected repo\n- `Ctrl+C` / `Ctrl+Q` — quit\n\n**Filtering:** `orderedRepos(query)` does a case-insensitive substring match on the alias, then applies the existing active-first ordering. When the query changes, `setQuery` resets the cursor to the top so the selection stays valid. Empty results show \"No matches.\"; no repos at all still shows \"No repos yet.\"\n\n**Layout:** a bordered search box (with a 🔍 prompt and a block cursor) sits between the panel and the footer, spanning the width. Placeholder text \"search…\" shows when empty.\n\nTwo honest caveats to verify with `go run .` (I can't render it):\n- I sized the search input at `width - 4` and the panel at `height - 5`; if the search box or panel overflows or leaves a gap on your terminal, the border/padding constants may need a small tweak. Tell me what you see.\n- The \"cursor\" is a static `▏` glyph appended to the text, not a real blinking terminal cursor. If you want a genuine cursor, bubbletea v2's `View.Cursor` field can position one, but the glyph approach is simpler and needs no coordinate math.\n- The 🔍 emoji is double-width; if it renders oddly in your terminal I can swap it for a plain `/` or `>` prompt.\n\nWant me to adjust any of the sizing, or is this good to test?"

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Now I have the full picture. Let me first give you my recommendation on structure before splitting anything, since \"one file per component\" isn't quite the right axis for a bubbletea app.\n\n**My recommendation on how to split**\n\nBubbletea's architecture is Model-Update-View, not components. A \"component\" (like the tab bar or search box) isn't a self-contained object here — its *state* lives in the model, its *input handling* lives in `Update`, and its *rendering* lives in `View`/`theme.go`. So splitting purely \"one file per component\" would scatter each component's logic across the same three concerns anyway.\n\nA cleaner split for this codebase is **by responsibility**, which is exactly what you asked `ui.go` to become. I'd suggest:\n\n- **`ui.go`** — just the bubbletea wiring: the `model` struct, `initialModel`, `Init`, `Update`, `View`, and `CreateProgram`. This is the \"initialize and update the UI\" role you want. `Update` and `View` stay here but become thin — they delegate.\n- **`repos_tab.go`** — everything specific to the Repos tab: `orderedRepos` (filter+sort), `launchSelectedRepo`, `renderReposTab`, and the repo-list navigation helpers. This is the biggest chunk of domain logic and the most likely to grow.\n- **`tabs.go`** — the `Tab` type, `tabTitles`, `nextTab`/`prevTab`, and `renderPlaceholder` for the empty tabs.\n- **`search.go`** — search state behavior: `setQuery` and the query-editing logic. (The *rendering* `SearchBox` can stay in theme or move here — see below.)\n- **`theme.go`** — stays as the pure styling layer (styles + render helpers). No change needed.\n\nThat gives `ui.go` a single job, and each tab/feature its own file. As you add the Chats tab later, it becomes `chats_tab.go` and `ui.go` doesn't grow.\n\n**One design decision worth making explicitly:** right now rendering is split awkwardly — `theme.go` has `TabBar`, `RepoRow`, `SearchBox` (styled *primitives*), while `ui.go` has `renderReposTab`, `renderPlaceholder` (which *assemble* primitives using model state). That's actually a reasonable boundary: theme = stateless styled primitives; the `render*` methods = model-aware assembly. I'd keep that boundary and just move the `render*` methods next to their tab logic. So `SearchBox` stays in `theme.go` (stateless primitive), but `setQuery` moves to `search.go`.\n\nThis is a pure code-move refactor — no behavior change — so I can verify success simply: it must still build and vet, and `gofmt` clean. \n\nDoes this responsibility-based split (rather than strict one-file-per-component) sound right to you? If so I'll do the moves: `ui.go` slimmed to bubbletea wiring, plus `tabs.go`, `repos_tab.go`, and `search.go`."
                  }
                ],

                    "data": "Builds, vets, and gofmt-clean.                     "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Builds, vets, and gofmt-clean.                     "data": "The panic is fixed and verified. I wrote a throwaway test that reproduced the exact crash conditions — a zero-value `model` (matching the all-zeros model in your stack trace) calling `renderReposTab(-9)`, `renderReposTab(0)`, and `View()` with width/height 0. It **passed** (no panic), then I removed the test file.\n\nRoot cause: on the very first render, before bubbletea sends the initial `WindowSizeMsg`, `m.height` is 0. `View` computed `panelHeight := m.height - 5 = -5`, then `panelInner` made `innerHeight` even more negative, and passed that straight into `renderReposTab` — which did `make([]string, 0, visibleRows)` with a negative capacity → `makeslice: cap out of range`. The `visibleRepoRows()` guard didn't help because `View` bypassed it and used the raw negative value.\n\nTwo layers of defense now:\n1. **`View`** returns early with an empty full-screen view when `m.width <= 0 || m.height <= 0`, so no negative-size math runs before the first resize message.\n2. **`renderReposTab`** clamps `visibleRows` to at least 1 as a backstop, so it's safe even if called directly with a bad value.\n\nBuilds, vets, and is gofmt-clean. Run `go run .` again — the crash on startup should be gone, and it'll render normally once the size message arrives (which is immediately)."

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "The rename logic is verified (tests then removed):\n- **Success + persistence** — renaming `api`→`backend` updates memory and writes `/src/api#backend` to disk in the correct `path#alias` format. ✓\n- **Empty rejected** — whitespace-only alias errors, original unchanged. ✓\n- **Collision rejected** — renaming to an existing alias (`web`) errors, original unchanged. ✓\n- **Same-name no-op** — renaming to the same alias succeeds silently. ✓\n\nHere's the feature as built:\n\n**`repos.Rename(old, new)`** — validates (non-empty, no collision), updates the alias, and persists.\n\n**`rename_dialog.go`** — a new file holding the dialog's state (`renameDialog`), input handling (`updateRenameDialog`), commit logic, and rendering (`renderRenameDialog`). Follows your file-per-responsibility structure.\n\n**Behavior:**\n- **`Ctrl+R`** on a selected repo opens a centered modal dialog, pre-filled with the current alias.\n- While open, the dialog is **modal** — it consumes all keys. Type to edit the alias, `Backspace` to delete, `←`/`→`/`Tab` to switch between **Save** and **Cancel** (focused button is highlighted).\n- **Enter** on Save commits the rename; on Cancel (or **Esc**) it closes without changing anything.\n- On a validation failure (empty or duplicate alias), the dialog stays open and shows a red error message so you can fix it.\n- On success, the cursor follows the renamed repo to its new sorted position.\n\n**Verification status:** The rename *logic* is test-verified. The *interactive dialog* (rendering, key routing, button focus) compiles/vets/gofmt-cleanly but needs a real TTY to confirm visually — please run `go run .`, select a repo, press `Ctrl+R`, and check the dialog looks right and Save/Cancel behave.\n\nTwo notes:\n- The dialog renders *in place of* the list (centered in the panel) rather than as a true floating overlay. That's the simpler, robust approach; lipgloss does have `NewLayer` for genuine compositing if you later want the dialog to float over a dimmed list.\n- Some terminals send `Ctrl+R` as a reverse-search sequence, but since bubbletea owns raw input in the alt screen, it should surface as `ctrl+r`. If it doesn't trigger, tell me and I'll confirm the exact key string."

                    "data": "I have the full picture now. `Add` upserts by alias (so a dir-name alias collision would silently overwrite a different repo's path — bad for this feature). Returns whether it was added.\n\n**`scan` logic (in the `repos` package, since it's domain logic):**\n- `ScanGitRepos(root) ([]string, error)` — walks `root`, returns paths of directories containing a `.git` entry, stops descending once a repo root is found, skips hidden/`node_modules` dirs.\n\n**UI — a new `add_dialog.go` modal wizard** with three phases (an `addPhase` enum):\n1. `phaseDir` — text input for the directory, pre-filled with `~/repos` (or home). Reuses the scrolling/windowing pattern from the repos list.\n\n**`ui.go` wiring:**\n- Model gets `adding bool` + an `addDialog` struct.\n- `Ctrl+N` opens the wizard (from the Repos tab).\n- New message types: `scanDoneMsg{paths, err}`.\n- When `adding`, input routes to the wizard (modal), like the rename dialog.\n\n**Alias default:** repo dir name, with collision-safe suffixing. User renames later with Ctrl+R as you said.\n\n**Verification:** I can unit-test `ScanGitRepos` (against a temp dir tree) and `AddRepo`/`HasPath` (dedup + alias disambiguation + persistence) without a TTY.                     "data": "A directory browser it is. That changes phase 1 from a text field to an interactive navigator. Actually, cleaner: `→`/`Enter` = enter dir, `←` = go up, and a labeled action to \"Scan here.\" Let me use **Enter to enter a directory** and **`Ctrl+S` / `s` to scan the current directory** — I'll show both hints in the footer.\n- Reuses the scrolling/windowing pattern from the repo list.\n\n**Phase 2 — Scanning:** async `tea.Cmd` walks the chosen directory. That finds repos a couple levels down (e.g. `repos/work/projectX`) without treating a repo's own subdirectories as candidates. \n\n**Phase 3 — Multi-select** results list: Space toggles, Enter adds selected (alias = dir name, path-dedup, alias-collision-safe suffix), Esc cancels.\n\n**`repos` additions:** `HasPath`, `AddRepo(path)` (dir-name alias, disambiguated), and `ScanGitRepos(root)` (recursive, stops at repo roots, skips hidden/`node_modules`).                     "data": "The `Row` helper prepends `\"  \"` or `\"› \"` (2 cells), so the label must be truncated to `contentWidth - 2`. Let me add a left-truncation helper and apply it. First the helper (in `add_dialog.go`, near the render code):"

                      "input": {
                        "__tool_use_purpose": "Add a left-truncation helper that fits a string to a max display width with a leading ellipsis.",
                        "command": "strReplace",
                        "newStr": "func (m model) renderAddSummary() string {\n\ttitle := dialogTitleStyle.Render(\"Repos added\")\n\tmsg := muted(\"Added \" + itoa(m.add.added) + \" repo(s).\")\n\treturn lipgloss.JoinVertical(lipgloss.Left, title, \"\", msg, \"\", Help(\"press any key to close\"))\n}\n\n// truncateLeft shortens s so its display width is at most max, keeping the\n// tail (most meaningful part of a path) and prefixing an ellipsis. It assumes\n// single-cell runes, which holds for filesystem paths.\nfunc truncateLeft(s string, max int) string {\n\tif max <= 0 {\n\t\treturn \"\"\n\t}\n\tif lipgloss.Width(s) <= max {\n\t\treturn s\n\t}\n\tif max == 1 {\n\t\treturn \"…\"\n\t}\n\trunes := []rune(s)\n\t// Keep the last (max-1) runes and prefix \"…\".\n\tkeep := max - 1\n\tif keep > len(runes) {\n\t\tkeep = len(runes)\n\t}\n\treturn \"…\" + string(runes[len(runes)-keep:])\n}",

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Both issues fixed and verified (tests removed):\n\n- **Width & height both stay constant while scrolling** — verified across all cursor positions in both the select phase and the browse phase; width and line-count are identical at every position.\n- **Full longest path shown untruncated** — no truncation, the box is exactly wide enough to fit `[x] ` + the whole longest path.\n\nThe truncation was fully undone, and I removed the width clamp so nothing gets cut off.\n\n**Root cause of the wrapping/height jump** (worth recording): lipgloss's `.Width(w)` sets the box's **total** width including border and padding, not the content width. So setting `.Width(86)` gave the content area only `86 − 2 border − 4 padding = 80` cells, and an 86-cell path row wrapped to two lines — which is why the height jumped from 12 to 11 depending on whether the long path was in view. The fix was to set `.Width(contentWidth + border + padding)`. This is the same lipgloss `.Width` semantics we hit earlier with the panel/search box, now applied consistently to the dialog.\n\nBuilds, vets, gofmt-clean. Run `go run .` → `Ctrl+N` → scan a directory with long paths and scroll — the box should keep a fixed size and show full paths."
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Performance is not a concern at all — this is a terminal UI redrawing a few dozen lines of text on keypress. There's no rendering cost worth worrying about; a side info panel adds a handful of string operations per frame. So go for it purely on UX grounds.\n\nLet me think about the layout and what to show, then confirm with you before building.\n\n**Layout:** split the panel area horizontally into two boxes side by side using `lipgloss.JoinHorizontal`:\n- **Left** — the repo list (narrower now, e.g. ~40% or a fixed width).\n- **Right** — an info panel for the highlighted repo.\n\nThe width math needs care: the two boxes plus their borders must sum to `m.width`. I'd give the list a share and the info panel the rest, both using the same `panelInner`-style border/padding accounting we already have. The search box and footer stay full-width below.\n\n**What to show in the info panel** — this is the real question. Options, given what a `Repo` currently holds (`Alias`, `Path`, `Session`):\n- **Alias** and full **path** (path is often truncated in the list, so showing it in full here is genuinely useful)\n- **Session status** — active/inactive, and the session ID if running\n- Cheap **git info** read live from the repo: current branch, dirty/clean, last commit. This is the most valuable content, but it means running `git` (or reading `.git/HEAD`) per highlighted repo. Reading `.git/HEAD` for the branch is basically free; running `git status` is heavier but still fine if done lazily (only for the highlighted repo, maybe cached).\n\n**A design decision to make:** how much git info, and how to fetch it.\n- **Minimal (zero cost):** alias, full path, session status, branch (read from `.git/HEAD` directly — a single small file read, no subprocess).\n- **Richer (small cost):** add dirty/clean and last-commit via `git`, run as an async `tea.Cmd` when the highlight changes so it never blocks the UI, with a cache keyed by path.\n\nMy recommendation: start with the **minimal, zero-subprocess** version (alias, path, session, branch from `.git/HEAD`). It's instant, needs no async machinery, and already makes the space useful. We can layer in async `git status` later if you want dirty-state/commit info.\n\nTwo things I want your call on before I build:\n1. **What content** — minimal (alias/path/session/branch) to start, or do you want the richer git status/last-commit now (async)?\n2. **Behavior on narrow terminals** — if the terminal is too narrow to fit both boxes reasonably, should I collapse back to the single full-width list? (I'd recommend yes, with a width threshold.)\n\nOnce you confirm those, I'll implement it."

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Good — git info it is: current branch and the last 5 commit titles. Let me think about how to fetch it, because that decision shapes the implementation.\n\n**Branch** — cheap: read `.git/HEAD`, which contains `ref: refs/heads/<branch>`. A single small file read, no subprocess. (Detached HEAD would contain a raw SHA; I'll handle that.)\n\n**Last 5 commit titles** — this needs `git log --format=%s -n 5`. That's a subprocess. Two ways to run it:\n- **Async** (`tea.Cmd`): fire it when the highlight changes, deliver results via a message, cache by path. Never blocks the UI even on a slow/large repo. More machinery.\n- **Synchronous**: run it inline in `View`/on cursor move. Simpler, but `git log` runs on every highlight change and *could* stutter on a huge repo or slow disk, and running it in `View` (which fires every frame) would be wasteful.\n\nThe right approach is **async with a cache**: when the highlighted repo changes, kick off a `tea.Cmd` that runs `git log` for that path; store the result keyed by path so re-highlighting is instant and we don't re-run. This keeps the UI responsive regardless of repo size.\n\n**Layout:** split the panel row into list (left) + info (right) via `JoinHorizontal`, with a width threshold to collapse to just the list on narrow terminals (you didn't object, and it avoids a cramped mess).\n\nHere's my plan:\n\n1. **`repos` package**: `GitBranch(path) string` (reads `.git/HEAD`) and `GitRecentCommits(path, n) []string` (runs `git log`). Both tolerate non-repos / errors gracefully.\n2. **`ui`**: an async `tea.Cmd` (`gitInfoCmd`) + a `gitInfoMsg{path, branch, commits, err}`, a cache `map[string]gitInfo` on the model, and logic to trigger the fetch when the highlighted repo's path changes.\n3. **Rendering**: an info panel (`renderRepoInfo`) showing branch + commit titles; `View` joins list + info horizontally, collapsing on narrow width.\n4. **Triggering**: on `moveCursor` and after launch/return, if the highlighted repo's info isn't cached, emit the fetch `Cmd`.\n\nOne implementation nuance: `moveCursor` currently returns nothing (it's called from the key switch which returns `m, nil`). To fire an async `Cmd` on highlight change, I'll have the relevant key cases return the `Cmd`. I'll compute \"did the highlighted repo change, and is its info uncached?\" and return `gitInfoCmd` when so.\n\nBefore I build — one quick confirmation: **collapse the info panel on narrow terminals** (below some width, show just the list), yes? And is a threshold around 80 columns reasonable, or do you want it always shown? Once you confirm I'll implement the whole thing."

                    "data": "All verified (tests removed):\n- **Git helpers** — against a real temp repo: `GitBranch` returns `main`, `GitRecentCommits` returns the last commits newest-first (`second commit`, `first commit`), and non-repo paths return empty gracefully. ✓\n- **Fetch dedup** — `ensureGitInfo` returns a `Cmd` the first time a repo is highlighted and `nil` afterward (no duplicate fetches). ✓\n- **Section rendering** — the panel shows the alias, `Branch`/`develop`, and `Recent commits`/commit titles. ✓\n\nFeature summary:\n\n**Layout** — when the terminal is ≥ 90 cols, the panel row splits into the repo list (left) and a 40-col info panel (right) via `JoinHorizontal`. Below that width it collapses to the full-width list.\n\n**Content** — the info panel shows the highlighted repo's alias, current **branch**, and **last 5 commit titles**.\n\n**Performance** — git data is fetched **asynchronously** (`tea.Cmd`) when the highlight changes and **cached per path**, so navigation never blocks and re-highlighting is instant. Branch is read straight from `.git/HEAD` (no subprocess); commits use `git log`.\n\n**Extensibility (as you asked)** — the panel is built from an ordered `infoSections` slice in `repo_info.go`.                     "data": "A settings form. Like the info panel, the key requirement is **extensibility** — a settings registry so adding a new setting later is a one-liner, not a rewrite. And a color theme dropdown means the theme's colors need to become runtime-switchable, not hardcoded `var`s.\n\nBefore I build, two design decisions worth surfacing:\n\n**1. Persistence.** Should settings persist across restarts? A color theme that resets every launch is annoying. I'd persist to `~/.taco/settings` (same dir as `repositories`). This means a small settings store in a new package, loaded at startup like `repos.Init()`.\n\n**2. Making the theme switchable.** Right now `colorAccent`, `colorBorder`, etc. are package-level `var`s initialized once. For a theme dropdown to work, selecting a theme must **reassign** these (or route all styles through a current-theme lookup). The cleanest approach: define a few named themes (each a set of colors), keep a \"current theme\" that the style helpers read from, and rebuild/reassign the styles when it changes. Since your styles are built once at package init, I'll refactor them to derive from the active theme so switching re-applies everywhere.\n\n**3. Extensible settings model.** A registry like the info panel: each setting is a descriptor (key, label, type, options, current value getter, and an apply function). The form renders each descriptor generically and routes input to the focused one. Adding a setting = append a descriptor. For now, one entry: Color Theme (a dropdown/enum).\n\nHere's my proposed plan:\n\n- **New `settings` package** — holds the persisted values (`map[string]string` or typed struct), `Init()`/`load`/`save` to `~/.taco/settings`, and a getter/setter. Mirrors the `repos` package pattern.\n- **Themes** — define named themes (e.g. `Default`, `Ocean`, `Mono`) as color sets in `theme.go`. Introduce an active theme the style helpers read from, and an `ApplyTheme(name)` that reassigns the color vars + rebuilds styles.\n- **`settings_form.go` (UI)** — a modal, opened with `Ctrl+P`, built from an extensible `[]settingField` registry. Each field has a label, a way to render its control (dropdown for enums), and input handling. `↑`/`↓` move between fields, `←`/`→` or `Enter` cycle a dropdown's value, `Esc`/save closes. The color-theme field applies + persists on change.\n- **Wiring in `ui.go`** — `settingsOpen bool`, `Ctrl+P` opens, modal routing, render centered in the panel.\n\nDecisions I want your call on before I write it:\n\n1. **Persist settings to `~/.taco/settings`?** (I strongly recommend yes.)\n2. **How should the dropdown apply** — live as you cycle it (instant preview), or only on an explicit \"Save\"? I'd suggest **live apply** (you see the theme change immediately) with the value persisted on close. Simpler and more satisfying than a save button.\n3. **Theme names** — I'll invent a few (Default/pink, Ocean/blue, Forest/green, Mono/grayscale). OK, or do you have specific palettes in mind?\n\nConfirm those three and I'll build it."
                  }

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "All verified (tests removed):\n- **Persistence** — `Set`/`Get` work, and settings survive a reload from disk (`~/.taco/settings`). ✓\n- **Theme cycle applies + persists** — cycling the theme field changes the active theme *and* writes it to settings; wrap-around returns to the start. ✓\n- **Unknown theme ignored** — a bad theme name doesn't corrupt state. ✓\n\nFeature summary:\n\n**Global settings modal — `Ctrl+P`** opens it from any tab; `Esc`/`Enter`/`Ctrl+P` closes. `↑`/`↓` move between settings, `←`/`→` change the focused setting's value. Currently one setting: **Color theme** (Default / Ocean / Forest / Mono), applied **live** as you cycle and **persisted** to `~/.taco/settings`.\n\n**Extensibility (as required):**\n- *Settings*: add an entry to the `settingFields` registry in `settings_form.go` — each field declares its label, options, current value, and a live `apply` hook. The form renders and edits any field generically. No other code changes needed for a new dropdown-style setting.\n- *Themes*: add an entry to the `Themes` slice in `theme.go` and it automatically appears in the dropdown.\n\n**Theme plumbing:** colors are now driven by an active `Theme`; `rebuildStyles`/`rebuildThemedStyles` reassign every color-dependent style in one pass when the theme changes, so switching re-tints the whole app instantly.\n\n**Startup:** `main.go` calls `settings.Init()` and applies the saved theme, so your last choice is restored on launch.\n\nBuilds, vets, gofmt-clean.\n\n**Verification status:** settings persistence, theme switching, and cycling logic are test-verified. The modal's live re-tinting and rendering need a real TTY — please run `go run .`, press `Ctrl+P`, cycle the theme with `←`/`→`, and confirm the whole UI recolors immediately; then quit and relaunch to confirm the theme persisted."

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "That's fair — it's worth pausing on before committing, because it's the biggest change we've discussed and it adds real ongoing complexity.                   {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "That's a really useful clarification — and it changes the picture entirely. What you're describing isn't grouping repos, it's having **multiple entries pointing at the same repo path but with different working contexts** (one on `master`, one for an old branch). That's a per-entry attribute, not a folder structure.\n\nAnd here's the thing: your data model **already supports the same path appearing more than once** — repos are keyed by alias, not path. So you can already have:\n- `access.diameter` → `/repos/access.diameter`\n- `access.diameter-legacy` → `/repos/access.diameter`\n\nBoth point at the same directory; they're just different tmux sessions with different aliases. The only friction is that the tmux session opens on whatever branch the working tree is currently on — there's no notion of \"this entry should be on `master`, that one on the old branch.\"\n\nSo the feature that actually serves your use case isn't group-tabs — it's **an optional branch per repo entry**. When you launch an entry that has a branch set, the tmux session does a `git checkout <branch>` (or better, `git worktree`) so each entry lands on its intended branch.\n\nTwo ways to implement that, with a real tradeoff:\n\n1. **Checkout on launch** — the session runs `git checkout <branch>` in the repo before starting the shell. Simple, but both entries share one working tree, so they'd fight over the checked-out branch if used at once.\n\n2. **Git worktrees** — each entry gets its own worktree directory for its branch (`git worktree add`). This is the *correct* model for \"work on master and an old branch simultaneously\" — separate directories, separate branches, no conflict. More moving parts (managing worktree dirs), but it genuinely does what you want.\n\nGiven your example (\"one for master, one for old branches\"), worktrees are the real answer — that's exactly the problem `git worktree` was designed for.\n\nBut I don't want to over-engineer based on a \"maybe.\" So let me ask: is this an actual workflow you have now, or a hypothetical? If it's real and you want to work two branches at once, I'd build the **branch-per-entry with worktrees** path. If it's speculative, I'd hold off entirely — your current \"same path, different alias\" already covers having two sessions, and we can add branch handling when the need is concrete.\n\nWhich is it — real need now, or maybe-someday?"
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Yeah, worktrees fit taco really naturally — it's already a \"pick a directory, get a tmux session\" tool, and a worktree is just another directory. Let me lay out the design space with the tradeoffs, since how you model worktrees shapes the whole UX.\n\n**The core idea:** a git repo can have multiple *worktrees* — separate directories, each checked out to a different branch, all sharing one `.git`. taco is perfectly positioned to be the thing that lists them and drops you into a tmux session for each. So instead of one list entry per repo, a repo can *expand* into its worktrees.\n\n**Three ways to model it in the UI, from lightest to richest:**\n\n**Option A — Worktrees as an info-panel section (read-only).**\nThe info panel already shows branch + commits. Add a \"Worktrees\" section listing the repo's existing worktrees (`git worktree list`). Purely informational to start. Tiny change, zero new modals. It surfaces the concept without committing to management. Good first step to see if it's useful.\n\n**Option B — Expandable repo → worktree sublist.**\nA repo row can expand (e.g. `→` on it, now that arrows are free) to show its worktrees indented beneath. Selecting a worktree and pressing Enter opens a tmux session *in that worktree's directory*. This is where taco becomes genuinely useful for your \"master + old branch\" case: each worktree is its own session, its own directory, no branch conflicts. `←` collapses. This reuses your existing list/scroll/session machinery — a worktree is just a path to launch.\n\n**Option C — Full worktree management.**\nEverything in B, plus actions to **create** a worktree (`git worktree add <dir> <branch>` — a dialog: pick/enter a branch, choose location) and **remove** one (`git worktree remove`, with your existing confirm-dialog pattern). This makes taco a full worktree manager: from the list you spin up a new worktree for a branch and immediately get a session in it.\n\n**How launching changes:** today `launchSelectedRepo` uses `repo.Path`.                     "kind": "text",
                    "data": "You've hit the classic config-vs-code tradeoff, and you actually proposed both solutions in one message. Let me give you my honest take, because I think the answer is \"both, layered\" — and the reasoning matters for how we structure it.\n\n**The key question: who is the flexibility for?**\n\n- **A `providers.json` config file** gives flexibility to the *end user at runtime* — they can add or tweak providers without recompiling. That's valuable if you expect users (or future-you) to bolt on arbitrary chat CLIs by editing a file.\n\n- **A Go provider interface + per-provider implementations** gives flexibility to the *developer* — adding a provider is a new struct implementing the interface. This is cleaner for anything that needs *behavior*, not just data.\n\nHere's the thing that decides it: some provider details are **pure data** (command string, sessions dir, agents dir), but others are **behavior** that a config file can't express. For example:\n- \"After resuming, how do we know which session file is the new one?\" — that's logic (snapshot dir, diff, parse output), not a string.\n- \"How do we list agents?\" — might be reading a dir, might be parsing a command's output. Varies per provider.\n- \"How do we start a session in directory X with agent Y?\" — command *templating* with substitution rules that differ per CLI.\n\nA `providers.json` with just four string fields will hit a wall the moment a second provider does something structurally different from kiro (different resume mechanism, different agent discovery). You'd end up cramming logic into config, which never ends well.\n\n**My recommendation: an interface as the source of truth, config as an optional override layer.**\n\n1. Define a Go `Provider` interface — the contract taco needs:\n   ```go\n   type Provider interface {\n       Name() string\n       StartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd      // new chat\n       ResumeCommand(sessionFile string) *exec.Cmd    // resume\n       SessionsDir() string\n       ListAgents() ([]string, error)                 // behavior, not just a dir\n       // how a new session file is identified after start\n   }\n   ```\n2. Ship a `kiroProvider` struct implementing it — all kiro-specific details live in code, where logic belongs.\n3. **Optionally** load `~/.taco/providers.json` to *override the data-ish fields* (command, dirs) for a known provider, or to define a *simple* generic provider that follows the common shape. Create it with kiro defaults on first run so it's discoverable/tweakable, but the code implementation is what actually drives behavior.\n\nThis gives you: clean behavior in code, user-tweakable data in config, and no pretending config can express logic it can't.\n\n**But** — and this is worth saying — even that might be more than you need *right now*. You have exactly one provider (kiro). The pragmatic path is:\n\n- **Build the `Provider` interface + `kiroProvider` implementation now.** This is the part that pays off immediately: it isolates all the kiro-specific commands/paths behind a clean seam, so the Chats-tab code (list, new, resume, pick agent) is written against the interface, not against kiro directly. Adding a second provider later = one new struct.\n- **Defer `providers.json` until a real second provider (or a real need to override) exists.** Once the interface is in place, adding a config loader that overrides fields is a small, additive change. Building it now is speculative — you'd be designing a config schema for providers you can't yet describe.\n\nSo: **interface + kiro implementation now, config file later.** You get the extensibility seam without guessing at a schema prematurely — same reasoning as when we deferred the group-tabs feature.\n\nThere's one blocker before any of this, though: I still need to know **kiro-cli's actual commands** — how to start a new chat (with a working dir and an agent), how to resume a specific session, and how session files are named/discovered. The interface's methods are shaped by those real commands. I started to check your system for the kiro binary but you cancelled it.\n\nSo, two things from you:\n1. Do you agree with **interface + kiro implementation now, `providers.json` deferred**? (Or do you specifically want the config file built now regardless?)\n2. What are kiro-cli's real commands — start-new (with dir + agent), resume-by-session, and how the session file/agent list is obtained? Either tell me, or let me run `kiro --help` / inspect `~/.kiro/sessions/cli` and `~/.kiro/...agents` to find out."

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Yes, the concept is the same as Java, but Go implements it differently in a few important ways. Let me map it out since you're coming from that mental model.\n\n**Same core idea:** you define an interface (a contract of methods), and a concrete type implements it. Code depends on the interface, not the concrete type, so you can swap implementations. That part is identical to Java.\n\n**The big difference: Go uses _implicit_ (structural) implementation — there's no `implements` keyword.**\n\nIn Java you write:\n```java\npublic class KiroProvider implements Provider {\n    public String name() { ... }\n}\n```\nThe `implements Provider` is explicit — you declare the relationship.\n\nIn Go, a type satisfies an interface **automatically** just by having the right methods. There's no declaration:\n```go\ntype Provider interface {\n    Name() string\n    StartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd\n}\n\n// No \"implements\" anywhere. kiroProvider satisfies Provider\n// simply because it has these methods with matching signatures.\ntype kiroProvider struct{}\n\nfunc (p kiroProvider) Name() string { return \"kiro-cli\" }\nfunc (p kiroProvider) StartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd { ... }\n```\n\nIf `kiroProvider` has all the methods `Provider` requires, it *is* a `Provider` — the compiler figures it out at the point where you use it as one. This is called structural typing (or \"duck typing, checked at compile time\").\n\n**Other differences from Java worth knowing:**\n\n- **No classes.** Go has structs (data) + methods attached to them. There's no class hierarchy, no `extends`. Composition replaces inheritance.\n- **Methods can be on any type**, not just structs — and they're defined *outside* the type body (the `func (p kiroProvider) Name()...` syntax).\n- **Interfaces are usually small.** Idiomatic Go favors tiny interfaces (often 1–3 methods). A common saying is \"the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction.\" Java interfaces tend to be larger and declared up front.\n- **A common convention:** you often add a compile-time assertion to make the \"implements\" relationship explicit *for readers* (optional, but nice):\n  ```go\n  var _ Provider = (*kiroProvider)(nil)\n  ```\n  This line does nothing at runtime — it just makes the compiler error if `kiroProvider` ever stops satisfying `Provider`. It's the closest Go gets to Java's `implements` as documentation.\n\nSo for taco: I'd define a `Provider` interface with the methods the Chats feature needs, write a `kiroProvider` struct that has those methods, and the Chats-tab code would hold a `Provider` value (currently always the kiro one). Swapping providers later = write another struct with the same methods. Practically the same design you'd do in Java, just without the ceremony.\n\nDoes that clear it up? If so, I still need kiro-cli's actual commands (start-new with dir + agent, resume, how session files/agents are found) before I can shape the interface — want me to probe your system for them, or will you tell me?"

                    "data": "Now I have the real formats. Key facts:\n- **Session id**: the JSON has `\"session_id\": \"<uuid>\"` and the filename is `<uuid>.json`. There's noise to skip: `.DS_Store`, `agent_config.json.example`, and subdirectories.\n- **Session detection**: since new sessions get auto-generated UUIDs, taco must **snapshot** the sessions dir before launch and **diff** after to find the new `.json`. The chat runs *inside tmux*. taco doesn't directly wait for kiro — it hands off to tmux (via `tea.ExecProcess`), and kiro creates its session file while you're in there. So the capture-the-new-session-id must happen **after you detach** from that tmux session (when taco resumes), by diffing the sessions dir against the pre-launch snapshot.\n\nThere's an ambiguity worth flagging: if kiro spawns **subagents**, one chat can create *multiple* session files (I can see `\"session_created_reason\": \"subagent\"` in that very file). So a naive \"one new file = the session\" diff could pick the wrong one. The most reliable identifier is the **main** session — the one whose `cwd` matches the directory you launched in and whose `session_created_reason` is *not* `subagent`. Session start/resume run **inside tmux** (so they get a real terminal and persist), consistent with how repos launch.\n\n**`chats` package** (mirrors `repos`): persists `~/.taco/chats` as `chatName#sessionID` (I'll store the **session id**, not the full path, since the path is derivable as `<sessionsDir>/<id>.json` and the id is what `--resume-id` needs).                     "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Good catch — you're right, there's a `\"title\"` field in the session JSON (it was `null` in that particular one because it was a fresh subagent session, but kiro does populate it on real chats). That changes chat naming for the better: instead of asking you to type a name, taco can **read the title from the session file** and use that as the chat name. Less friction, exactly your \"as little manual hassle as possible\" principle.\n\nSo the flow becomes: **pick agent → pick directory → launch**. No name prompt. On return, taco finds the new session file, reads its `title`, and stores the entry. Clean.\n\nBut `title` being `null` at creation time is the wrinkle I need to handle. When you *first* start a chat and immediately detach, kiro may not have set a title yet (it's often derived from your first message). So at capture time the title could still be `null`. I'll handle it gracefully:\n- If `title` is set → use it as the chat name.\n- If `title` is null/empty → fall back to something readable (e.g. the directory name + short id, or just \"untitled\"), and — better — **re-read the title from the file each time the Chats list renders**, so once kiro sets it, taco picks it up automatically without you doing anything.\n\nThat last point is actually the cleaner model: rather than freezing the name at capture time, taco stores the **session id/path** as the entry's identity and derives the **display name from the live title** in the file. So the list always reflects kiro's current titles, and renamed/late-titled sessions just show correctly. This also means taco's `chats` file could store just the path (as you specified: `chatName#path`) — but the `chatName` there becomes a cached/fallback, with the live title preferred.\n\nLet me confirm the title-handling approach before I build, since it shapes the chats store:\n\n**Option A (store name, static):** capture the title at creation, write `chatName#path`, never update it. Simple, but if the title was null at capture or changes later, the list is stale.\n\n**Option B (store path, derive name live):** the entry's identity is the path/session-id; the display name is read live from the file's `title` each render (falling back to the stored name or a placeholder if null). Always accurate, self-updating. Slightly more work (a small JSON read per listed chat, cheap and cacheable).\n\nI lean toward **B** — it matches how kiro actually works (titles appear/change over time) and needs no manual renaming. Your `chatName#path` format still works as the persisted fallback.\n\nWhich do you want — A (simple, static name) or B (live title from the file)? Once you pick, I'll start building the provider interface + kiro implementation."

                    "data": "Everything builds, vets, and is gofmt-clean across the whole module.\n\nHere's the Chats feature as built, with your requested provider abstraction:\n\n**Provider abstraction (interface + impl, no config file):**\n- `provider.Provider` — the contract (start, resume, sessions dir, list agents, snapshot/detect-new-session, live title/cwd).\n- `kiroProvider` — implements it with your real commands: new chat = tmux session running `kiro-cli --agent <agent>`; resume = tmux session running `kiro-cli chat --resume-id <id>`. Adding another provider later = one new struct.\n\n**Chats store (`~/.taco/chats`):** persisted as `name#sessionID`; identity is the session id, display name is the **live title** read from the session file (Option B), falling back to the stored name.\n\n**Chats tab:**\n- Lists saved chats (searchable/scrolling), each labeled by its live title.\n- **Space** → new-chat wizard: **agent picker** → **directory browser** (starts at `$HOME`, `Ctrl+S` to start here) → launches kiro in tmux via `tea.ExecProcess`.\n- On return, taco **diffs the sessions dir** to find the newly-created session, correctly preferring the main session over subagents, reads its title, and records it.\n- **Enter** on an existing chat → resumes it.\n- Chat tmux sessions are separate (`taco-chat-*`) and persist across taco exits, so you can resume.\n\n**Verified:** provider agent/session reading against your real `~/.kiro`, chats CRUD + persistence, and the full wizard→capture flow (including subagent/pre-existing filtering and live-title naming).\n\n**Needs a real TTY to confirm** (I can't drive interactive tmux/kiro from here): actually starting a kiro chat, detaching, and seeing it appear in the list; and resuming one. Please run `go run .`, go to the Chats tab (`Tab`), press Space, pick an agent, browse to a dir, `Ctrl+S`, chat, then detach — and confirm it shows up and resumes with Enter.\n\nOne thing I should flag honestly: the new-chat directory browser uses plain ASCII markers (`>`/`^`) rather than the emoji ones in the add-repos wizard, and the Chats list doesn't have the fixed-width/centering polish the repos list got. If you want the Chats tab to match the repos tab's visual treatment (info panel, alignment, etc.), that's a follow-up worth doing once you've confirmed the core flow works."
                  }

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Verified (tests removed):\n- **Extended format** `name#sessionID#agent` round-trips, and **legacy** two-field lines still parse (agent empty). ✓\n- **Table renders** with `Name`/`Agent`/`Directory` header and the chat rows, showing the agents (`worker`, `analyzer`) via the stored fallback when no live session file exists. ✓\n\nThe Chats tab now shows a table:\n- **Name** — live session title (fallback to stored name / \"untitled\")\n- **Agent** — live `agent_name` from the session file (fallback to the agent you picked at creation, which is now persisted as the third field `name#sessionID#agent`)\n- **Directory** — live `cwd` from the session file\n\nColumn widths are computed from **all** rows so the table doesn't shift while scrolling, there's a header row, and the selected row is highlighted as before. The store format is backward-compatible with any existing two-field entries.\n\nBuilds, vets, gofmt-clean, and the full module test run passes.\n\n**Verification status:** the table rendering, the agent/dir data resolution, and the extended persistence are test-verified. The live end-to-end (start a real chat, see it populate Name/Agent/Directory from the actual session file, resume it) still needs a real TTY — run `go run .`, `Tab` to Chats, and check the table looks right once you have some sessions. Note the columns aren't truncated yet, so a very long directory path could make a row wide; if that bothers you on real data I can add the same left-truncation/fixed-width treatment we used in the add-repos wizard."

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Sharp question — that exposes a real correctness issue with my fallback logic.\n\nIf you `/agent swap` mid-session, kiro updates `agent_name` in the session file to the new agent. So there are now **two disagreeing sources**: the live `agent_name` (new, correct) and taco's stored agent (the one you picked at creation, now stale).\n\nThe good news: my `chatAgent` helper already **prefers the live value**:\n```go\nfunc (m model) chatAgent(c *chats.Chat) string {\n    if a := m.provider.SessionAgent(c.SessionID); a != \"\" {\n        return a  // live agent_name — reflects the swap\n    }\n    return c.Agent // stored fallback\n}\n```\nSo after a swap, the table shows the **new** agent, because the live `agent_name` is non-empty and wins. That's the correct behavior — same Option-B philosophy as the title. The stored agent is only used when the live one is `null` (which we saw happens ~1 in 8 sessions).\n\nSo the display is already right. But there's a subtler question your example raises: **which agent should a stale stored fallback even represent?** Right now it's frozen at creation time. After a swap, if the live value later becomes `null` for some reason, taco would fall back to the *creation* agent, not the swapped-to one — mildly misleading. Two ways to tighten this:\n\n1. **Leave it** — the live value is almost always present and wins, so this only bites in the rare null case, and even then \"the agent you started with\" is a reasonable guess.\n2. **Refresh the stored agent** to match the live one whenever we read it and they differ, so the fallback stays current. A tiny write, but it means the persisted file self-heals toward the truth.\n\nMy honest take: the display is already correct for your `/agent swap` case, so this is a low-stakes edge. I'd lean toward **leaving it** (option 1) rather than adding write-on-read complexity for a rare null fallback — but if you'd rather the stored value track swaps, option 2 is easy.\n\nWant me to leave it as-is (live value wins, which handles the swap correctly), or add the self-healing refresh?"
                  }
                ],
