                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Good — glad it works live. Here's exactly how, top to bottom.\n\n**1. The agent lives in the session file, and kiro keeps it current.**\nWhen you `/agent swap`, kiro rewrites its session JSON (`~/.kiro/sessions/cli/<id>.json`), updating the nested field:\n```json\n{ \"session_state\": { \"agent_name\": \"worker\" } }\n```\nSo the file is always the source of truth — kiro maintains it, taco just reads it.\n\n**2. taco reads that field live, on every render.**\nIn the kiro provider, `SessionAgent` reads the file fresh each time it's called:\n```go\nfunc (k *kiroProvider) SessionAgent(sessionID string) string {\n    m, ok := k.readMeta(sessionID)          // reads & parses the JSON file\n    if !ok || m.SessionState.AgentName == nil {\n        return \"\"\n    }\n    return *m.SessionState.AgentName\n}\n```\n`readMeta` does an `os.ReadFile` + `json.Unmarshal` into a struct that mirrors the nested shape:\n```go\ntype sessionMeta struct {\n    ...\n    SessionState struct {\n        AgentName *string `json:\"agent_name\"`\n    } `json:\"session_state\"`\n}\n```\nIt's a `*string` (pointer) specifically so I can tell apart `\"agent_name\": null` (pointer is nil → return \"\") from an actual value.\n\n**3. The table calls it every time it draws.**\n`renderChatsTab` runs on every frame/keypress, and for each row it calls:\n```go\nfunc (m model) chatAgent(c *chats.Chat) string {\n    if a := m.provider.SessionAgent(c.SessionID); a != \"\" {\n        return a          // live value from the file — wins\n    }\n    if c.Agent != \"\" {\n        return c.Agent    // stored fallback (only if live is empty/null)\n    }\n    return \"—\"\n}\n```\n\nSo the chain is: **you swap → kiro rewrites the file → next time taco renders the table, it re-reads the file → the new agent shows up.** There's no caching and no stored state involved in the happy path — the display is always a fresh read of what kiro wrote. That \"read live every render\" is why it just works without taco needing to know a swap happened.\n\nThe stored agent (the `name#sessionID#agent` third field we added) is *only* a fallback for the rare case where the file's `agent_name` is `null`. In your swap case the live value is present, so it wins and the stored one is never consulted.\n\nOne honest caveat about the \"every render\" approach: it does a file read + JSON parse per visible row per frame. For a handful of chats that's completely negligible. If you ever had hundreds of chats visible and it felt sluggish, the fix would be to cache reads and invalidate on file mtime — but we're nowhere near needing that."
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Yes — for the *session's own state* (agent, title, working directory), the kiro JSON files are the source of truth, and taco treats them that way: it reads them live on every render rather than storing its own copy. kiro owns those files; taco just reflects them.\n\nBut it's worth being precise, because there are actually **two** sources of truth here with different roles:\n\n**kiro's session JSONs — source of truth for _session state_:**\n- `agent_name`, `title`, `cwd` — whatever kiro currently has. taco reads these fresh, so `/agent swap`, a title change, etc. show up automatically.\n\n**taco's `~/.taco/chats` file — source of truth for _which chats taco tracks_:**\n- This is the list of session IDs taco knows about, i.e. \"these are the chats you asked me to remember and want in the list.\" kiro has hundreds of session files (263 on your machine); taco only shows the ones recorded in `~/.taco/chats`.\n- The stored `name` and `agent` in that file are just **fallbacks** for when kiro's live value is missing (e.g. `title: null` right after creation, or a null `agent_name`).\n\nSo the division is: **taco's file decides _membership_ (what's in your list), kiro's files decide _content_ (what each row displays).** taco never duplicates kiro's state as the authority — it defers to the JSON and only keeps the minimum needed to (a) know the chat exists and (b) have a sensible fallback label.\n\nOne consequence worth knowing: because kiro's file is authoritative for content, if you were to delete a kiro session file, taco's row would fall back to the stored name/agent and show `—` for the directory (live lookup fails). And taco's list entry would still exist until you delete it from taco — the two files can drift, by design, since they answer different questions."
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Rename for chats — same pattern. `Ctrl+R` already renames repos, so I'll make it tab-aware. One thing to be clear about given our source-of-truth discussion: the display name prefers the **live kiro title**. So renaming a chat sets taco's stored fallback name, but if kiro has a live title, that title still wins in the display.\n\nThat's a real UX wrinkle worth deciding: if you rename a chat to \"My deploy\" but kiro's title is \"Deploy pipeline\", the table will still show \"Deploy pipeline\" (live title wins). Two options:\n\n1. **Rename sets the stored fallback only** — consistent with the current model, but your rename may appear to \"not take\" if kiro has a title.\n2. **A renamed chat's stored name overrides the live title** — i.e. once you explicitly rename, taco shows your name regardless of kiro's title.\n\nFor a rename feature to feel like it works, **option 2** is what users expect — an explicit rename should stick and be shown. I'll implement it so that if a chat has a user-set name, `chatDisplayName` prefers it over the live title. I'll need a flag to distinguish \"auto-captured name\" from \"user-renamed name.\"\n\nLet me confirm this is what you want before building: **should renaming a chat make your name take precedence over kiro's live title?** (I recommend yes — otherwise rename looks broken.) Assuming yes, I'll add a \"renamed\" flag to the chat entry (persisted), and `chatDisplayName` prefers the stored name when that flag is set.\n\nWant me to go with that (rename overrides live title), or keep it as a fallback-only rename?"
                  }

That's partly why you added manual rename. So before investing in local inference, it's worth asking whether auto-retitling actually improves the find-and-resume workflow or just adds churn and a heavy dependency.\n\n**A much cheaper middle ground that might get you 80% of the value:** instead of an LLM, derive a better title from the conversation *heuristically* — e.g. show the **most recent user prompt** (or first line of it) rather than the *first* one, optionally truncated. It updates as the conversation evolves, needs zero models, and is trivially cheap. It's not \"smart,\" but \"what did I last ask here\" is often a better find-me signal than \"what did I first ask.\"\n\nMy recommendation, in order:\n1. **Try the heuristic first** (latest user message as the title) — near-zero cost, no dependency, and see if it's actually good enough.\n2.                     "data": "Got it — a taco-owned, taco-managed background process (spawned, supervised, and killed by taco, invisible to the user) is acceptable to you. That reframes it: it's not \"the user runs another process,\" it's \"taco has a helper it manages.\" Fair distinction.\n\nThat opens the door to the Python-sidecar approach. But before I build, let me lay out the real design so we're aligned, because a supervised sidecar has moving parts and I want to pin the decisions.\n\n**Architecture:**\n- A small Python HTTP server (FastAPI/uvicorn or even stdlib `http.server`) that loads **SmolLM2** (via `transformers`) once at startup and exposes `POST /title` taking recent messages, returning a title.\n- taco spawns it on launch as a child process, waits for a health check, calls it over `127.0.0.1:<random-port>`, and **kills it on exit** (using the same signal/cleanup machinery we built for tmux sessions).\n- Title generation runs **async** (a `tea.Cmd`) every N prompts using a sliding window of the last ~10 messages, result cached and used as the chat's display name (behind the same `TitleFor` seam, overriding kiro's title but not a user's manual rename).\n\n**The decisions I need from you, because they determine feasibility on real machines:**\n\n1. **Python dependency management.** The sidecar needs Python + `transformers` + `torch`. How should that get onto the machine?\n   - (a) Assume the user has Python and taco `pip install`s deps into a venv it manages under `~/.taco/` on first run.\n   - (b) Ship a bundled/frozen Python (PyInstaller) so no system Python is needed — much bigger artifact, more complex build.\n   - (c) Assume the user already has the deps.\n   \n   This is the crux. (a) is the usual approach but means a first-run that creates a venv and installs `torch` (hundreds of MB). There's no free lunch on this — SmolLM via transformers pulls in torch.\n\n2. **Model download.** SmolLM2 weights (~100–350 MB depending on size) download from HuggingFace on first use, cached in `~/.taco/models` (or HF cache). Acceptable one-time cost?\n\n3. **Which SmolLM size** — 135M (fastest, weakest), 360M (good balance), or 1.7B (best titles, heavier)? For titles I'd suggest **360M-Instruct**.\n\n4. **Failure behavior.** If Python/deps aren't available or the sidecar fails to start, taco should degrade gracefully — fall back to kiro's title (and/or the pure-Go heuristic) and never block the UI. Agree?\n\nHere's my honest concern to weigh: the heaviest, most fragile part isn't the Go↔Python plumbing — it's **getting `torch` + `transformers` reliably installed across users' machines**. SmolLM2-360M, and the `llama-cpp-python` (lighter) engine rather than torch?\n4. graceful fallback when unavailable?\n\nOnce you confirm these four, I'll build it: the Python sidecar script, the venv/model bootstrap, the Go supervisor (spawn/health-check/kill-on-exit), and the async title generation wired into the chat display-name seam."

                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Let me clear up a misconception, because there's no magic \"just run it\" package that avoids an engine — but there's an important nuance about what you're actually avoiding.\n\n**There's no `pip install smollm2` that \"just runs.\"** SmolLM2 is model *weights*, not a runnable program. To run it in Python you always need three things: (1) an inference **engine**, (2) the **weights**, (3) a **tokenizer**. The question is only *which* engine, and how the weights arrive.\n\nBut — and this is the good news for your concern — **none of the reasonable options need API keys or Ollama.** The API-key/cloud stuff is a totally separate world (calling OpenAI, etc.). Everything we're discussing is fully local. So you can drop that worry entirely; local inference never involves keys.\n\nWhat you *can't* drop is \"download the weights once.\" That's unavoidable — the model has to exist on disk. Where they come from:\n\n- **`transformers`** (`pip install transformers torch`): `AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(\"HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct\")` — this auto-downloads the weights from HuggingFace the first time (no key needed for public models), caches them, and every run after is offline. So it *feels* like \"just run it,\" but the first call fetches ~700 MB and it drags in `torch`.\n\n- **`llama-cpp-python`** (`pip install llama-cpp-python`): you point it at a `.gguf` file. You still have to get that GGUF once (download it, or bundle it). Lighter than torch, but not \"keyless magic\" — you still supply the model file.\n\nSo the honest picture: **no engine avoids the one-time weights download, and none of them need API keys or Ollama.** The \"does it feel like just-run-it\" difference is:\n- `transformers` → the download is automatic/implicit on first use (closest to what you're imagining), but heaviest install (torch).\n- `llama-cpp-python` → you manage the GGUF file explicitly, but the install is far lighter.\n\nThere's also **`mlx-lm`** on your Mac specifically (`pip install mlx-lm`, `mlx-community/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct`): Apple-Silicon-native, fast, auto-downloads weights, no torch, no keys. Since you're on macOS, this is actually the nicest \"just run it\" option — but it's Mac-only, so taco would be Mac-only for this feature (or fall back elsewhere).\n\nSo to answer directly: **yes, you can run SmolLM2 in Python with no HuggingFace account, no Ollama, no API keys** — but you *do* pick an engine (`transformers`, `llama-cpp-python`, or `mlx-lm`) and accept a one-time weights download. The closest to your \"just `llm-smollm2` and go\" mental model is `transformers` (auto-download, implicit) or `mlx-lm` on Mac (auto-download, lightweight, fast).\n\nGiven the taco-owned-sidecar plan, which engine do you want the sidecar to use?\n- **`transformers`** — most \"just works,\" heaviest install (torch).\n- **`mlx-lm`** — lightest + fastest on your Mac, auto-downloads, no torch; Mac-only.\n- **`llama-cpp-python`** — light + cross-platform, but you manage the GGUF file.\n\nIf taco is mainly for you on macOS, `mlx-lm` is honestly the sweet spot. If it needs to work on Linux too, `transformers` or `llama-cpp-python`. Tell me which, and whether cross-platform matters, and I'll build the sidecar around it."

                    "data": "Good question to circle back on — and honestly, for *titles specifically*, pure-Go NLP gets you further than you'd expect, without any of the sidecar/model/download weight. Let me be straight about what it can and can't do.\n\n**What pure-Go NLP realistically achieves for a title:**\n\nThe task isn't \"understand the conversation\" — it's \"surface the few words that best identify this chat so I can find it in a list.\" That's an **extractive keyphrase** problem, and classic NLP handles it decently:\n\n- **TextRank / TF-IDF keyphrase extraction** over a sliding window of recent messages → pulls out the most salient terms/phrases. E.g. a conversation about fixing token expiry in auth middleware might yield `auth token expiry` or `middleware token refresh`. Topical, updates as the conversation evolves, entirely deterministic.\n- **Noun-phrase extraction** (light POS heuristics) → grabs phrases like \"the login redirect loop\" rather than scattered keywords, reading a bit more naturally.\n- **Frequency + recency weighting** → weight terms in recent messages higher, so the title tracks where the conversation currently *is*, not just where it started (which was your whole complaint about kiro's first-prompt titles).\n\nAll of this is a few hundred lines of Go, no dependencies, no cgo, no process, no download, runs in microseconds. It fits your original idea exactly: sliding window → recompute every few prompts → cache.\n\n**What it honestly can't do:**\n\n- It won't produce a fluent, human-sounding title like \"Debugging the OAuth redirect loop.\" It produces *keyphrases* — `oauth redirect loop` — not sentences. Usually fine for a list label, but it's not \"smart.\"\n- It can be fooled by boilerplate/code-heavy messages (lots of tokens that aren't the topic). Mitigable with stopword lists and code-fence stripping, but not perfect.\n- No abstraction — it can only surface words that actually appear. If the conversation is *about* authentication but never says \"auth,\" it won't infer it.\n\n**My honest assessment:** for the specific goal of \"a stable-ish, topic-indicative label that beats kiro's frozen first-prompt title,\" a pure-Go **recency-weighted keyphrase extractor** is genuinely a good fit and probably 70–80% as useful as a tiny LLM for this narrow task — at ~1% of the complexity.                   {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "All verified (tests removed):\n- **Titler uses both roles + recency** — with a 5-user + 5-assistant window, the recent cross-role topic (ingress/routing) wins over the older one. ✓\n- **Retitle on detach persists** — after a chat session detaches, a generated title is produced from the transcript and saved. ✓\n- **Precedence is correct**: manual rename > generated title > kiro live title > stored fallback. ✓\n- **Manual rename is never clobbered** — re-detaching after a rename keeps the user's name. ✓\n\nHere's the feature as built:\n\n**When you detach from a chat session** (new or resumed), taco reads that session's `.jsonl` transcript, takes the **last 5 user messages and last 5 assistant messages**, and generates a keyphrase title (recency-weighted, user intent weighted higher, code/stopwords stripped). It's stored as the chat's `GenTitle` and shown in the table.\n\n**Precedence** in the Name column: your manual rename wins; else the generated title; else kiro's live title; else the stored fallback. So titles now **evolve as the conversation grows** (regenerated each detach) without you renaming — which was your original goal — while manual renames stay sticky.\n\nNew plumbing: `titler` package (pure Go, no deps), `provider.SessionTranscript`, `chats.GenTitle` + `SetGenTitle` (persisted as a 5th field, backward compatible).\n\nBuilds, vets, gofmt-clean, all packages tested.\n\n**Honest caveat on quality:** as we saw against your real transcripts earlier, the extractive titles are topical keyphrases, not fluent sentences, and can pick up noise from code-heavy or short conversations. This is the ceiling of pure-Go extraction. It's wired behind the same seam we discussed, so if the quality disappoints in real use, the SmolLM sidecar remains a drop-in upgrade for `retitle()` later. \n\nRun `go run .` → start or resume a chat, have a short conversation, detach, and check the title reflects the recent discussion. If the titles feel too keyword-y, tell me and we can either tune the extractor (bigrams, better code stripping) or revisit the model path."
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Right — that's the fundamental limit I flagged: extractive keyphrase methods can only surface words that literally appear, so you get `deployment pipeline build` rather than \"Fixing the deployment pipeline.\" No amount of tuning the pure-Go approach changes that — it can't *phrase* anything, only pick words. If keyword-strings aren't what you want, we've hit the honest ceiling of the dependency-free path.\n\nSo this is a real decision point, and I don't want to keep polishing something that structurally can't give you what you're after. The options, honestly:\n\n1. **Accept keywords, but make them read better.** Cheap tuning within pure Go: extract **bigrams/noun-phrases** (keep adjacent word pairs like \"deployment pipeline\" together), better code stripping. You'd get `deployment pipeline · auth tokens` instead of scattered single words. Still not sentences, but less \"bag of words.\" Small effort, no dependencies.\n\n2. **Go to a real model for fluent titles.** This is the SmolLM sidecar we scoped — a taco-owned Python process using `llm-gguf`, generating actual phrases like \"Debugging the deployment pipeline.\" It's the only way to get genuinely fluent, abstractive titles. Cost: the venv bootstrap + one-time GGUF download + managed subprocess we discussed. It drops into the same `retitle()` seam — literally swap `titler.TitleFromFile(...)` for a call to the sidecar.\n\n3. **A middle option I should mention honestly: kiro itself.** You already have a capable LLM installed — `kiro-cli`. Instead of a whole new model/sidecar, `retitle()` could shell out to kiro non-interactively with a \"summarize into a 3-5 word title\" prompt over the transcript window. No new dependency, no download, no sidecar lifecycle — it reuses the tool that's already there. The cost is a subprocess call per retitle (a few seconds), but it's async on detach so it wouldn't block you. This might genuinely be the best fit: real LLM quality, zero new infrastructure.\n\nMy honest recommendation has shifted now that you've seen the keywords: **option 3 (use kiro-cli to generate the title)** is probably the sweet spot for you. You wanted \"within taco / no extra processes to install,\" and kiro is already installed and is a strong model — so `retitle()` runs `kiro-cli` with a titling prompt on the recent messages, async, and you get fluent titles with none of the SmolLM sidecar's install/download/lifecycle baggage. The keyphrase titler we built stays as an instant fallback if kiro isn't available or is slow.\n\nBefore I build option 3, I need to know how to invoke kiro-cli **non-interactively** to get a one-shot completion (a prompt in, text out, no TTY/session). You gave me the interactive commands earlier (`kiro-cli --agent`, `kiro-cli chat --resume-id`), but not a \"run this prompt and print the answer\" form. Does kiro-cli have something like `kiro-cli chat --no-interactive \"prompt\"` or `echo \"prompt\" | kiro-cli`? If you tell me the non-interactive invocation (or let me check `kiro-cli chat --help`), I'll wire `retitle()` to call it.\n\nWhich direction do you want:\n1. Tune the pure-Go extractor toward phrases (cheap, still keyword-ish),\n2. SmolLM sidecar (fluent, heavy), or\n3. **Use kiro-cli to generate the title** (fluent, no new deps) — my recommendation?"

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "Good question to raise, and let me give you an honest architectural take rather than jump at \"build our own,\" because that path is a trap here.\n\nFirst, let me separate two things tmux is doing for you, because they have very different alternatives:\n\n1. **Persistence** — the kiro process survives after you detach, so you can resume it. This is the *hard* requirement, and it's exactly what tmux is for.\n2. **Terminal handoff** — taco suspends, kiro takes the real terminal (via `tea.ExecProcess`), you interact, then taco resumes.\n\nThe \"snappier\" alternatives you mention address different parts, and each has a serious catch:\n\n**\"A bubbletea terminal emulator\" (embedding kiro inside taco's TUI).**\nThis means taco spawns kiro on a PTY and renders its output *inside* a bubbletea pane (there are libraries like `vt10x`/`darkforest`-style VT emulators, and Charm has experimented with this). Honest problems:\n- **You'd be writing/embedding a full VT100 terminal emulator.** kiro-cli is itself a rich TUI (colors, cursor moves, its own alt-screen, resizing). Rendering that correctly inside *another* TUI means emulating escape sequences, scrollback, resize propagation — this is genuinely hard and a common source of glitchy rendering. It would almost certainly feel *less* snappy and *more* buggy than tmux, not more.\n- **Persistence is lost.** If kiro runs as taco's child in an embedded pane, killing taco kills kiro. You'd have to re-add tmux (or a daemon) underneath anyway to keep resume working. So it doesn't remove tmux — it stacks a hard emulation problem *on top* of it.\n\n**\"Build our own\" (a custom session manager / daemon).**\nTo match tmux you'd need: a background daemon that owns PTYs, keeps processes alive after detach, handles resize, reattach, scrollback... that *is* tmux. Reimplementing it is a multi-month project and you'd ship a worse tmux. This is the classic \"don't rebuild the thing that already solves your hard problem\" case.\n\n**So where's the actual snappiness cost today?** It's worth being precise, because tmux itself is not slow — the latency you might feel is likely from:\n- `tea.ExecProcess` doing a full suspend/restore of taco's alt-screen around the handoff, and\n- tmux's `new-session -A` spinning up a fresh session with all your bindings each time.\n\nThose are tunable *without* abandoning tmux.\n\n**My honest recommendation — keep tmux, but reduce the friction:**\n\n1. **Direct handoff, thinner wrapper.** Your current command builds a whole tmux session with escape bindings, mouse mode, etc. every launch. That setup work adds startup latency. You could pre-configure those in a tmux config once and make the launch command minimal (`tmux new-session -A -s <name> kiro-cli ...`), so attach/resume is near-instant.\n\n2. **Question whether kiro sessions even need tmux persistence.** Here's the key insight: kiro already persists its **conversation** to disk (the session files — that's how resume works via `--resume-id`). So for a *chat*, you may not need the tmux **process** to survive at all — when you \"resume,\" you're starting a fresh kiro that reloads the saved conversation by id. If that's true, chats don't need tmux for persistence the way repo shells do. You could run kiro **directly** via `tea.ExecProcess` (no tmux), and \"resume\" is just `kiro-cli chat --resume-id` in a direct handoff. That's genuinely snappier — no tmux layer for chats at all — and kiro's own persistence covers resume.\n\nThat last point is the real lever. **Repos** need tmux (a long-lived shell you return to). **Chats** might not — kiro's `--resume-id` reloads state from disk, so the running process surviving detach may be unnecessary. If so, we drop tmux for chats entirely, run kiro directly, and it'll feel much snappier.\n\nBefore I'd change anything, I want to verify that assumption rather than guess: does `kiro-cli chat --resume-id <id>` fully restore a conversation started in a *previous, already-exited* kiro process (i.e. persistence is on-disk, not in the running process)? If yes, chats don't need tmux and we simplify to a direct `ExecProcess` launch. If resume only works while the process is alive, then tmux (or equivalent) is genuinely required.\n\nTwo questions:\n1. Does `kiro-cli chat --resume-id` reload a conversation whose kiro process has fully exited? (I'd bet yes, given the session files — but you'd know.)\n2. For chats specifically, do you actually need the kiro process to keep *running* in the background while detached, or is reload-from-disk on resume sufficient?\n\nIf reload-from-disk is sufficient (likely), my recommendation is: **drop tmux for chats, run kiro directly via `tea.ExecProcess`, resume via `--resume-id`** — simpler and snappier — and keep tmux only where it's actually needed (repo shells). Want me to look into that direction?"
                  }

                  {
                    "kind": "text",
                    "data": "That's a smart reframing, and it correctly identifies the real cost: N separate tmux sessions each cold-starting kiro-cli. One master session that stays warm and you switch conversations *within* it is the right instinct. But let me make sure the mechanism actually holds up, because there's a subtlety that decides whether this works.\n\n**The key question is: can a single running kiro-cli switch between conversations in-place?**\n\nYour plan assumes: one tmux session, kiro-cli loaded once, then \"run the commands to resume whatever session we want within that one.\" That only works if kiro-cli, *while already running*, can swap its active conversation to a different `--resume-id`. That's an **in-process** capability — does kiro-cli have a slash-command or input to switch conversations mid-session (e.g. `/resume <id>` or similar)?\n\n- **If yes** — kiro can switch conversations while running — then your master-session idea works beautifully: one warm tmux session, taco sends it the switch command, snappy.\n- **If no** — `--resume-id` is only a startup flag — then \"resume within the running session\" isn't possible without restarting kiro, which brings back the cold-start you're trying to avoid. In that case the master session doesn't help, because switching conversation = restarting kiro = the same initialization cost.\n\nSo the architecture hinges on a kiro-cli feature I don't know exists. Before I build anything, that's the thing to pin down. Do you know if kiro-cli can switch to a different saved conversation *from within* a running session (a command you type into it), rather than only via the `--resume-id` launch flag?\n\nThere's also a second issue even if in-session switching exists: a master session shows **one conversation at a time**. If you resume chat A, then chat B, then attach to the master session, you see B. That's fine for \"jump to the conversation I picked,\" but taco's model of \"each chat is its own thing you attach to\" changes — there's one screen, and taco drives which conversation it's showing. Workable, just noting the model shift.\n\nTwo honest possibilities depending on kiro's capability:\n\n1. **kiro can switch conversations in-session** → build exactly what you described: one persistent `taco-chats-master` tmux session running kiro; to open/resume a chat, taco sends kiro the switch command (via `tmux send-keys` or kiro's own mechanism) then attaches you to the master session. One warm process, snappy switching. This is the ideal.\n\n2. **kiro can only resume at launch** → the master session can't switch conversations without restarting kiro, so it doesn't save the cold start. The realistic snappiness win then is different: keep per-chat sessions but **pre-warm** or **thin the launch** (minimal tmux config, no per-launch binding setup), or accept the cold start.\n\nSo: **does kiro-cli let you switch to another saved conversation while it's already running?** If you know the command, tell me; if not, I can check `kiro-cli chat --help` / kiro's in-session slash commands to find out. That answer determines whether the master-session design is viable or whether we optimize a different way. I don't want to build the master-session plumbing on an assumption that kiro can't actually switch in-process."
                  }

                    "data": "That's a reasonable call — better to remove it cleanly than keep something whose UX you're not happy with. The core friction (per-session kiro cold-start, no clean in-process conversation switching) is a real limitation, not something we can polish away, so cutting it is honest.\n\nBefore I start deleting, let me confirm the scope so I remove exactly what you want and nothing you'd regret:\n\n**Remove entirely:**\n- The **Chats tab** (list/table, search, new-chat wizard, resume, rename, delete) — `chats_tab.go`\n- The `chats` package (`~/.taco/chats` persistence)\n- The `provider` package (interface + kiro impl) — it existed only for chats\n- All chat-related model state, key routing, footer hints, and the `chatFinishedMsg` plumbing in `ui.go`\n- Chat initialization in `main.go`\n\n**Keep:**\n- Everything Repos-tab (list, search, sessions, add/rename/delete, info panel, worktree-free)\n- Settings + themes\n- The `session`/`commands`/`repos` packages\n\n**One decision:** the tab bar currently has three tabs — **Repos, Chats, Coming Soon**.           {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "That's a reasonable call — better to remove it cleanly than keep something whose UX you're not happy with. The core friction (per-session kiro cold-start, no clean in-process conversation switching) is a real limitation, not something we can polish away, so cutting it is honest.\n\nBefore I start deleting, let me confirm the scope so I remove exactly what you want and nothing you'd regret:\n\n**Remove entirely:**\n- The **Chats tab** (list/table, search, new-chat wizard, resume, rename, delete) — `chats_tab.go`\n- The `chats` package (`~/.taco/chats` persistence)\n- The `provider` package (interface + kiro impl) — it existed only for chats\n- All chat-related model state, key routing, footer hints, and the `chatFinishedMsg` plumbing in `ui.go`\n- Chat initialization in `main.go`\n\n**Keep:**\n- Everything Repos-tab (list, search, sessions, add/rename/delete, info panel, worktree-free)\n- Settings + themes\n- The `session`/`commands`/`repos` packages\n\n**One decision:** the tab bar currently has three tabs — **Repos, Chats, Coming Soon**. With Chats gone, do you want:\n- (a) **Repos + Coming Soon** (just drop Chats), or\n- (b) **Repos only** (drop both Chats and the Coming Soon placeholder, leaving a single-tab or no-tab-bar UI), or\n- (c) **Repos + Coming Soon**, renaming/repurposing later?\n\nAlso: should I **delete the `~/.taco/chats` file** handling entirely (the file itself, if it exists on your disk, would just become orphaned — harmless, I won't touch your data unless you ask)?\n\nTell me the tab choice (a/b/c) and I'll do the full removal, verifying it still builds/vets/fmt-clean and that no Chats references remain. My default if you don't specify: **(a)** keep Repos + Coming Soon, leave any existing `~/.taco/chats` file on disk untouched."

                  "data": "package ui\n\nimport (\n\ttea \"charm.land/bubbletea/v2\"\n\t\"charm.land/lipgloss/v2\"\n\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/provider\"\n)\n\n// sessionFinishedMsg is sent when a tmux session (run via tea.ExecProcess)\n// exits and the bubbletea program resumes.\ntype sessionFinishedMsg struct {\n\terr error\n}\n\ntype model struct {\n\tactiveTab Tab\n\n\t// Terminal dimensions, updated on every resize.\n\twidth  int\n\theight int\n\n\t// Repos tab state.\n\trepoCursor int\n\trepoScroll int    // index of the first visible row (scroll offset)\n\tquery      string provider.Provider\n\tchatCursor  int\n\tchatting    bool\n\tchat        chatWizard\n\tchatDelete  bool\n\tchatDelData chatDeleteData\n\tchatRename  bool\n\tchatRenData chatRenameData\n\n\t// launchedAlias is the repo whose session was most recently launched,\n\t// so the cursor can follow it after the list reorders.\n\tlaunchedAlias string\n\n\t// Rename dialog modal state.\n\trenaming bool\n\tdialog   renameDialog\n\n\t// Add-repos wizard modal state.\n\tadding bool\n\tadd    addDialog\n\n\t// Delete-confirmation modal state.\n\tdeleting bool\n\tdel      deleteDialog\n\n\t// chatFinishedMsg struct {\n\tdir    string\n\terr    error\n\tresume bool\n}\n\nfunc initialModel() model {\n\treturn model{\n\t\tactiveTab: TabRepos,\n\t\tprovider:  provider.NewKiro(),\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc (m model) Init() tea.Cmd {\n\treturn nil\n}\n\nfunc (m model) Update(msg tea.Msg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {\n\tswitch msg := msg.(type) {\n\tcase tea.WindowSizeMsg:\n\t\tm.width = msg.Width\n\t\tm.height = msg.Height\n\t\t// Load git info for the initially selected repo.\n\t\treturn m, m.ensureGitInfo()\n\n\tcase gitInfoMsg:\n\t\tif m.gitCache i\n\t\t\t\t\tbreak\n\t\t\t\t}\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tm.clampScroll(len(ordered))\n\t\t\tm.launchedAlias = \"\"\n\t\t}\n\n\tcase scanDoneMsg:\n\t\tm.onScanDone(msg)\n\n\tcase chatFinishedMsg:\n\t\tm.onChatFinished(msg)\n\n\tcase tea.KeyPressMsg:\n\t\tkey := msg.String()\n\n\t\t// Settings is a global modal: it opens from any tab and consumes keys.\n\t\tif m.settingsOpen {\n\t\t\tm.updateSettings(key)\n\t\t\treturn m, nil\n\t\t}\n\n\t\t// When the rename dialog is open it is modal: it consumes all keys.\n\t\tif m.renaming               "content": [
                {
                  "kind": "text",
                  "data": "package ui\n\n// Tab identifies a top-level view in the UI.\ntype Tab int\n\nconst (\n\tTabRepos Tab = iota\n\tTabChats\n\tTabComingSoon\n)\n\n// tabTitles are the labels shown in the tab bar, in order.\nvar tabTitles = []string{\"Repos\", \"Chats\", \"Coming Soon\"}\n\n// nextTab / prevTab cycle through the tabs.\nfunc (m model) nextTab() Tab {\n\treturn Tab((int(m.activeTab) + 1) % len(tabTitles))\n}\n\nfunc (m model) prevTab() Tab {\n\treturn Tab((int(m.activeTab) - 1 + len(tabTitles)) % len(tabTitles))\n}\n\n// renderPlaceholder is shown for tabs with no content yet.\nfunc (m model) renderPlaceholder(name string) string {\n\treturn muted(name + \" — nothing here yet.\")\n}"
                }
              ],
              "status": "success"
            }
          }
        ],

                  "kind": "text",
                  "data": "package main\n\nimport (\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"os\"\n\t\"os/signal\"\n\t\"sync\"\n\t\"syscall\"\n\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/chats\"\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/commands\"\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/repos\"\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/settings\"\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/ui\"\n)\n\nfunc initializeRepos() {\n\tif err := repos.Init(); err != nil {\n\t\tfmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, \"error: \", err)\n\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t}\n}\n\n// initializeSettings loads persisted settings and applies the saved theme.\nfunc initializeSettings() {\n\tif err := settings.Init(); err != nil {\n\t\tfmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, \"error: \", err)\n\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t}\n\t// Apply the persisted color theme (defaults to \"Default\" if unset).\n\tui.ApplyThemeByName(settings.Get(\"theme\", \"Default\"))\n}\n\n// initializeChats loads the saved chat sessions.\nfunc initializeChats() {\n\tif err := chats.Init(); err != nil {\n\t\tfmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, \"error: \", err)\n\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t}\n}\n\n// cleanupOnce guards terminateAllSessions so it runs at most once, whether\n// triggered by the deferred call or the signal handler.\nvar cleanupOnce sync.Once\n\n// terminateAllSessions kills every tmux session started during this run.\nfunc terminateAllSessions() {\n\tcleanupOnce.Do(func() {\n\t\tfor _, repo := range repos.WithSessions() {\n\t\t\tcmd := commands.TerminateSession(repo.Session.ID)\n\t\t\tif err := cmd.Run(); err != nil {\n\t\t\t\tfmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, \"failed to terminate session %s: %v\\n\", repo.Session.ID, err)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\trepo.Session = nil\n\t\t}\n\t})\n}\n\nfunc main() {\n\tinitializeRepos()\n\tinitializeSettings()\n\tinitializeChats()\n\n\t// Normal-exit and Ctrl+C path: bubbletea catches SIGINT itself and\n\t// returns from Run(), so a deferred cleanup covers both.\n\tdefer terminateAllSessions()\n\n\t// Backstop for signals bubbletea does not handle (e.g. SIGTERM): run\n\t// cleanup, then exit. Ctrl+C (SIGINT) is normally consumed by bubbletea,\n\t// but we listen for it too in case the program is not in the UI loop.\n\tsigCh := make(chan os.Signal, 1)\n\tsignal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)\n\tgo func() {\n\t\t<-sigCh\n\t\tterminateAllSessions()\n\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t}()\n\n\tprogram := ui.CreateProgram()\n\n\tif _, err := program.Run(); err != nil {\n\t\tfmt.Printf(\"Error: %v\", err)\n\t\tterminateAllSessions()\n\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t}\n}"

            "data": "The Chats feature is fully removed. Final state verified:\n\n- **Builds, vets, gofmt-clean**, all packages compile.\n- **No residual references** to chats, provider, or any chat symbols anywhere in the Go source.\n- **Packages remaining**: `commands`, `repos`, `session`, `settings`, `ui` — the `chats` and `provider` packages are gone.\n- **Tabs**: `Repos` + `Coming Soon`, exactly as you asked.\n\nWhat was removed:\n- `ui/chats_tab.go`, the `chats/` package, the `provider/` package\n- All chat model state, the `chatFinishedMsg`, chat modal routing, chat key bindings, chat footer hints, and the chat render case in `ui.go`\n- Chat initialization in `main.go`\n- The leftover chats selected-row style in `theme.go`\n\nWhat's intact and unchanged:\n- Repos tab: searchable/scrolling list, tmux sessions, add wizard, rename, delete, git info panel\n- Settings + themes\n- Session cleanup on exit\n\nTwo housekeeping notes:\n- `go mod tidy` ran, so any now-unused dependencies from the chat/provider code were pruned from `go.mod`/`go.sum`.\n- I left your data and stray files alone: an existing `~/.taco/chats` file (if any) is untouched and simply unused now, and I didn't touch `chat.md` / `session_commands.txt` in the repo.\n\ntaco is back to a focused repos-and-tmux tool with the Coming Soon placeholder for whatever you build next."
